Date April 1 1940.
Subject Seven Leftist leaders released during hostilities in 1937.
Made by and Forwarded by Supt. Tan Shao Liang

It is correct that Shen Chun Ju(沈君儒),
Chang Nai Chi(章乃器 ), Wong Tsao Shi(王造時),
Li Kung Po(李公樸), Chow Tao Ren(鄒韜奮),
Sha Chien Li(沙千里 ) and Shi Liang(史良 ),(female

authorities in Shanghai in anti-Japanese and pro-

EVENING ECHO

MAR 27 1940

“7 GENTLEMEN”
GET POSITIONS
IN CHUNGKING

Using the struggling plank of the
'United front to resist the Japan-
ese", the professionals known in
Shanghai in pre-war days as the
"Seven Gentlemen", have at last
obtained suitable berths in the
Chungking government, a new ar-
rival stated this morning.
It is recalled that Shen Chun-ju,
Chang Nai-chi, Wang Tsao-shi, Li
Kung-po, Chow Tao-fen, Sha
Chien-li and Shi Liang were thrown
into gaol by order of Gen. Chiang
Kai-shek when they launched a vi-
gorous campaign calculated to ex-
ert pressure on the National Gov-
ernment to wage war on Japan.
Flirt With Communists
With a weekly mouthpiece called
"Life", these leaders had flirted
with the Communists and instigated
disturbances among the students,
shop-keepers and labourers.
When hostilities started, they
were released from incarceration
and given substantial government
positions, it was gathered.
Chang Nai-chi is said to have
been made director of the finance
department of the Anhwei Provin-
cial government, while the rest are
reported to be in Chungking serving
with several departments.
All seven, it was pointed out, are
members of the People's Political
Council.
However, nothing has so far been
heard about the progress of their
movement, the informant observed.

SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE

The Dismissal Of
Student Leaders

A special prerogative of the Chinese
educational authorities which the public
has never questioned, is that of eliminat-
ing from the register, at the start of the
summer vacation, those students who
failed to make good in the past academic
year.

At the commencement of the present
summer vacation, several schools in the
Peiping and Tientsin area expelled a
number of students. We learn that the
majority of those dismissed were con-
nected with the patriotic student move-
ment of last winter. It is reported that
one university in Peiping gave two grand
demerits each to the leaders for their
agitation against the annual examination
and that as a result several of them
were expelled.

If this report is true, we feel that
the measures taken by the authorities
call for reconsideration.

Education is a means of discovering
the strong points of a person and de-
veloping those points so as to make him
or her a useful member of society. One
student may be very good in his studies
but lacking in executive ability. Con-
versely, another student may be quite
backward in his studies but able to lead
others.

The purpose of modern education is
not to train all men to be scholars or
scientists but to find out the talents of
each one and develop them accordingly.
That student leaders possess certain
special qualifications goes without saying.
They may not be very brilliant scholars
but they certainly have gifts of leader-
ship otherwise they would not have been
elected to that position by their fellow
students. We do not deny that the
authorities have valid grounds for dis-
missing these leaders, for they violated
certain regulations of their schools, but
at the same time, it must be pointed
out that if every student were law-
abiding and made no mistakes education
would lose its very justification and
raison d'etre. We feel that in dismissing
students for having assumed the leader-
ship of the student patriotic movement
the educational authorities have de-
parted from the true functions of education
and should take the consequences of the
action into consideration. We therefore
urge the authorities to reconsider
their action. — Ed. (Trans.)

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Monday, June 22, 1936

Student Safety
Measures Taken

Japanese Say Student
Trouble Fostered
By Reds

Chinese authorities in Shanghai today continued precautionary measures to prevent further demonstrations in echo of the Southwest's clamor for an "anti-Japanese" expedition.

To prevent recurrence of demonstrations such as that held at the North Station yesterday morning, large forces of police are stationed near the railway depot. Trains, however, have been running as usual since 3 o'clock yesterday afternoon.

Crowds Gather

A crowd of more than 600 persons, including many students and women, demonstrated at the North Station and sought to commandeer trains to proceed to Nanking to appeal for a war with Japan. They displayed a banner identifying themselves as members of the "Shanghai All-Circle National Salvation Association," the same one which staged an anti-Japanese meeting at the Chamber of Commerce building on May 30, the anniversary of the "Nanking Road Incident."

They arrived at the North Station at 7:20, seeking to board the morning express for Nanking at 8. Halted by officers, they resorted to speech-making and slogan-shouting. They later left the station for Hsin Ming Road where they dispersed.

Nippo Sees Dirty Work

The hand of the Southwestern authorities, 'anxious to foster unrest close to the capital, while Nanking is maneuvering to split the Kwangtung-Kwangsi alliance,' was seen today by the Shanghai Nippo in yesterday's student demonstrations at the North Station.

Commenting on the "anti-Japanese and national salvation" appears voiced by the students, "apparently in accord with the Southwestern slogans," the Nippo termed the agitation "improper."

Agitators Said Active

"Behind the movement," said the paper, "stand professional anti-Japanese agitators and Communists, who are trying to create a rift between Nanking and Japan."

Simultaneously, the movement is utilized by the Southwest, which complements its military moves by political maneuvers, said the journal.

"Sincerity" Wanted

The Nippo expressed its concern over the use of anti-Nipponese slogans by the Chinese. "The Chinese authorities," it said, "should exhibit more sincerity and live up to their international obligations by controlling such demonstrations."

The Nippo blamed the students' behavior on the influence of the Southwest and the readjustment of Sino-Japanese relations.

"The Chinese Government," the Nippo declared, "should take appropriate measures to prevent professional agitators from taking into their hands the control of the student movement."

Peiping Movement Ends

The Peiping Student trouble, which flared up last year following the autonomy movement in East Hopei, and again recently, as a result of the increase of Japanese troops in North China, came to a quiet end yesterday as all schools completed their final examinations. The majority of the students immediately left for their homes for the summer holidays.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES. TUESDAY, JUNE 23, 1936 -

Students Launch Campaign
To Improve Rural Life

Trial Will Be Made Of The Plan In Kiangsu And
Chekiang This Year; Promotion Of Public
Health In Villages Big Feature

NANKING, (by mail).—"Go to the rural districts"—this will be the watchword of college and high school students this summer.

Under the sponsorship of the New Life Movement Association in Nanking, a movement has been launched for students to utilize their summer vacation to improve rural life in various villages in Kiangsu and Chekiang in accordance with the new life principles laid down by General Chiang Kai-shek, President of the Executive Yuan, who is the founder of the New Life Movement.

The programme of the movement will include the improvement of the living conditions of the farmers, heightening of their cultural level, promotion of public health in village life, and enforcement of the new life creed.

Students who are willing to undertake the rural improvement work are asked to register with the Association. They will be put under the control of teachers of their respective schools, who will in turn receive constant instructions from the Association.

Public Lectures

In the execution of the programme the students will take special pains to impress the importance of a sanitary and decent living on the farmers. They will give public lectures on public health, and sanitation, and the old Chinese virtues, "Li, Yi, Lien and Chih" or etiquette, justice, conscientiousness and integrity.

They will also visit barber shops, tea houses, inns and other public places to propagate the "New Life" ideas.

Girl students will approach the families of the peasants to talk to them on the same subjects.

This summer the student service movement will be confined to Kiangsu and Chekiang. If it proves successful, it will be extended to other provinces next year.—Central News.

TWO TRAINS ARE HELD UP; CROWD

Traffic at the North Railway Station was disrupted yesterday morning and two trains were not permitted to leave as per schedule when some 500 students of both sexes, reinforced by other elements, besieged the station and demanded transportation to Nanking, where they wanted to petition the Government to "declare war on Japan at once." THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS WEDNESDAY, MARCH 11, 1936

LORD MARLEY ON STUDENT RIOTS

His Information on Shanghai Queried in the Lords:
Lord Stanhope's Promise

FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT

London, Feb. 6.
Lord Marley asked a question in the House of Lords this week with regard to the International Settlement in Shanghai, and I quote below in full his question together with the answer and the discussion which ensued:

Lord Marley rose to ask His Majesty's Government whether they have any information regarding the alleged use of force against unarmed student demonstrators by the police (including British subjects) in the International Settlement in Shanghai in December, 1935; and to move for Papers.

The noble Lord said: My Lords, I make no apology for placing this Motion down at such very short notice, but I did give notice to the noble Earl who represents the Foreign Office. The object of the Motion is to suggest to him the information which it might be desirable for the Government to obtain, if they agree that it is desirable that we should know a little more about what is going on. During recent years there has been great activity in China on the part of the Japanese, which has aroused widespread opposition among patriotic Chinese, and this opposition has shown itself in a large number of demonstrations by Chinese students all over China. The reports from China show that these demonstrations have universally been entirely orderly. There has been no disorder. There has been no opposition by the police, and there has been no shooting or damage to life or limb. Reports from Canton, Tientsin, Szechuan, and Nanking all say the same thing. In particular, from present capital of China, the reports are that the discipline and self-control of the students and the police were admirable.

"North-China Herald" Quoted

When it comes to Shanghai we find that the earlier demonstrations by the students were entirely orderly. The students were received by the Mayor of Greater Shanghai, Mr. Wu Teh-chen, who promised them the support of the civic authorities in their complaints against Japanese depredations and their desire for the patriotic defence of their country. They were also supported by General Chiang Kai-shek, the Commander-in-Chief, who sent them a telegram saying that he was entirely of their opinion that it was desirable to organise nationally against Japanese depredations. The civic authorities in Shanghai even went to the length of putting the autobus service of that City at the disposal of the students to enable them to get back to their various colleges.

The report in regard to their demonstrations in Peking (or Peiping as it now called) is that the action of the police in firing on students was entirely due to the police themselves. I read in the "North China Herald" a few days ago the report of the special correspondent, who was an eye witness, and who said that the case had been extremely badly managed by the authorities. His words were these:

"Almost from the very start the police seemed to be bent on using force against perfectly peaceful demonstrators, and in many cases used unnecessary violence.

Position in Shanghai

The average age of the demonstrators in Peking, he says, was well below eighteen, both boys and girls, and the police were firing ball cartridge on these young people.

The Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs (Earl Stanhope): Can the noble Lord give me the date?

Lord Marley: The "North China Herald" of December 25, 1935. In Peking the Chinese police were under the control of the Japanese, and I suppose it is not unnatural that the Japanese should desire to repress what might he considered to be anti-Japanese demonstrations. But when it comes to Shanghai the matter is entirely different. The position in Shanghai was broadly this. Numbers of students from the Universities and schools assembled on December 24 at about nine o'clock in the morning in the Nanking Road. There have been a number of letters in the Press by eye-witnesses of what went on. They said that the foreign police in Shanghai were clearing the students, taking their banners from them, tearing them up, and trampling on them. There were indignant protests from foreigners who were watching what was going on, particularly because the demonstrators were mainly schoolboys and schoolgirls. One letter rather indicated the attitude of a certain few English people. The writer protested against these scholars parading in the International Settlement at all. If they wished to parade, he said, let them do so in the Chinese City. When you realise that Shanghai is a city of about 3½ million people, of whom only 9,000 are British, and the total number of foreigners is 50,000 or thereabouts, it indicates a most undesirable point of view on the part of British people living in other countries to claim that the Chinese have no right to demonstrate in their own City.

Extracts of Two Letters

I have a letter on this matter from two persons who themselves witnessed what went on. One is an American lady who is entirely trustworthy, and the other is a very eminent Chinese lady who is very well-known throughout the world and whose evidence cannot be but reliable. I venture to read extracts from this letter, because I think it is desirable that the view of eye-witnesses should be given. The letter says this:

"Moved by patriotic feelings, Chinese students from all schools and Universities in Shanghai, following the lead of students in other parts of China in resisting the dismemberment by Japanese actions, gathered for a peaceful demonstration in Nanking Road in the early morning of December 24. These students, many of them children of middle school age, were perfectly peaceful and orderly. They formed into groups according to their schools, and began distributing leaflets bearing national liberation slogans. There was no kind of disorder until suddenly a band of foreign police, armed with sticks and short truncheons, appeared and began an attack. Even a fully armed body of Sikh police arrived and joined in the attack.

"The students were absolutely unarmed. They had only leaflets, slogans, and banners. Despite this, one police officer whose cap and arm band bore the number B. R.M.P. began beating the students over the head. The other police followed his example, with the result that many students fell with blood streaming over their faces and from their mouths. We counted eleven unconscious students lying in their own blood. Even when unconscious and down, still the British police bent down and continued beating the prostrate forms. Riot vans appeared, and several students were arrested for assaulting the police. The boys and girls had only their bare hands, yet they were reported to have attacked and injured a number of British police officers.

"On the same day a British police officer of the name of Lovell arrested a student whom he charged with having assaulted and injured him. The boy was sentenced to fifteen days imprisonment, suspended for two years provided the boy showed good conduct. The Shanghai municipal police are reported to have appealed to a higher Court because of the leniency of the Chinese Court. It was never mentioned that the Chinese student was only fourteen years of age."

Goodwill of China

The question is really of greater importance than mere student demonstrations in a far distant city. May I remind the House that it is vital to Great Britain that we should have the good will of the Chinese people? Our trade with China is by no means unimportant, and if there is illwill on the part of the Chinese they are perfectly capable of applying boycotts to British goods such as they have applied to Japanese goods. I may venture to give figures, during the last five years, partly owing to the anti-Japanese boycott in China, the share of Japan in Chinese imports has dropped from 25 per cent. in 1930 to 14 per cent. in 1933 and 12 per cent. in 1934. In the same period, because of the good will the Chinese have for Great Britain, our trade has risen from 8 per cent. in 1930 to 11.3 per cent. in 1932 and 12.1 per cent. in 1934. I take these figures from the Department of Overseas Trade Report on Economic Conditions in China, 1933-35, just published. That document points out that the figures show that quite apart from the great potentialities of the Chinese market, the trade is already of sufficient value to merit the earnest attention of United Kingdom manufacturers and exporters. But however much our manufacturers and exporters pay attention to the details of their trade, they cannot trade if there is anti-British feeling among the Chinese people.

International Control

The Chinese may not be entirely well informed. I notice that habitually they talk of the "British" International Settlement in China, which is an entire misconception. The International Settlement is not British controlled in the same way as it was a few years ago; it is under international control. Nevertheless we always have talk of the "British" controlled police and the "British" International Settlement. If the Chinese think that the British police are using undue force to put down peaceful demonstrations by students who, if they demonstrated in a like way in this country, would receive the support of all right-thinking men and women, because they are merely showing their patriotism and their desire to defend their country against attack from outside, then that must tend to create resentment. For these reasons I hope the question in the form that I have put it may make clear the position. It is not necessary that we should take sides, but it

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, MONDAY, FEBRUARY 10, 1936

Students, Nantao Policemen
Clash Again At West Gate

Anti-Japanese Parade. And Demonstration Broken
Up By Batons; 300 Students Flee; 20 Hurt;
Five Arrested During Bitter Skirmish

Another clash between demonstrating Chinese students and police occurred yesterday afternoon, this time in Nantao, when approximately 300 students fought savagely with Chinese police officers of the Bureau of Public Safety after the police had attempted to break up a parade. Only one student was injured, though not seriously.

The students, most of whom were from Chinan University at Chefoo, went into Nantao yesterday afternoon and, after holding a number of mass meetings among idlers and loungers in that crowded quarter, they organized a parade with banners inscribed with anti-Japanese slogans. Shouting the slogans and gathering curious pedestrians into their train, they started marching through the Chinese city.

Cordon Formed

At the West Gate, they were met by a squad of policemen from the second division, Public Safety Bureau of the Municipality of Greater Shanghai. The officer in charge ordered the leaders of the students to disperse their followers. The leaders refused, and the march continued. More constables were then called out, as tension was growing and the students were getting into an ugly mood, defying police, shouting their slogans, etc. A cordon of police was hastily thrown across the students' path and the students themselves, hesitating, stopped their march for a moment. The leaders harangued them, urging that they show some fight. A huge crowd collected.

Finally at about 4.30 p.m. the students charged the police, attacking with whatever they could find—sticks, bricks, and such. Police did not draw arms, but met the attack with batons, which they wielded freely in the ensuing melee. The scuffle lasted for some time and the district was in utmost confusion as police and students battled together. The police, however, eventually got the upper hand, and as the students fell back, they realized they were defeated and the parade, now broken up, dispersed, the students fleeing into adjoining alleyways and scattering.

Score Injured

No police officers were injured, but it was estimated that about 20 students were hurt in the fight, mostly through blows on the head from police batons. Only one student was so badly hurt that he had to be taken care of. He was sent by ambulance to the Paulun Hospital, where he was treated for injuries to the head and hands, but later was released.

Five students were arrested by police during the skirmish, all being from a private Chinese school on Connaught Road. They were being detained in the Public Safety Bureau in Nantao last night. It is not known whether students from any other schools were involved in the affair.

SHANGHAI TIMES, TUESDAY, DECEMBER 31, 1935.

Fuh Tan Students To Make
Speeches In Shanghai

Meeting Held Yesterday Deliberates On Present
Situation; Chiang Kai-shek Secures Return Of
Chiaotso Youths; Train Held Up

At a meeting held yesterday students of the Fuh Tan University decided to form the Fuh Tan Student National Salvation Association and to send speech makers to the streets of Shanghai beginning from to-morrow in order to arouse the interest of the public in doing patriotic work. The street propaganda work will be continued for a week, it was decided.

The meeting also decided that the Association be divided into five departments requiring all students to participate in some one of them. A written petition to Dr. Li Deng-hui, President of the University who recently resigned because he was unable to prevent his students from going to Nanking, urging him to remain in office, was also resolved upon.

In conjunction with the youths of other schools the Fuh Tan group issued a long statement declaring that although the students did not reach Nanking they had made the Government and general public realize how serious the national crisis was which was their original aim. The pilgrimage to Nanking was only a means to an end, it was said.

Another Train Stopped

Apparently inspired by the Fuh Tan youths a large group of students in Changchow near Wusih tried to commandeer railway coaches in order to go to Nanking to protest against the autonomy movement in North China, and as a result the 1.30 p.m. train to Nanking from Shanghai was stopped at Changchow for a considerable time. The afternoon and night express trains left Shanghai according to the schedule.

Chiang's Persuasion
HSUCHOW, Dec. 30. — The group of students from the Technical College at Chiaotso, Honan, who came to Hsuchow two days ago with the intention of going to Nanking to present a petition to the Government regarding the North China situation, left here yesterday afternoon to return to Chiaotso.

Their decision to cancel their trip to the capital was made after the receipt of a telegram from General Chiang Kai-shek, president of the Executive Yuan, advising them to return to their studies.

General Chiang's telegram states that their patriotism is well appreciated by the Government and the people, but because of the fact that an interview has been arranged for January 15 in Nanking to hear the views of the students, it would not be necessary now for them to go to Nanking to the neglect of their studies.—Central News.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, FRIDAY, DECEMBER 27, 1935
19234

Lull Seen In Agitation By
Shanghai Student Bodies

Fuh Tan Students Proceed Fitfully To Nanking In
Train Seized Here; Incomplete Resumption Of
Train Services At North Station Yesterday

Following several hectic days
of demonstrating and agitating
against the "autonomy movement"
promoted by Japan in North
China, a distinct lull set in on
the Shanghai student front
yesterday, only minor demonstra-
tions taking place in Chapei and
Nantao. In the International
Settlement and French Conces-
sion all was quiet.

The focal point of interest in
the student movement, as far as
this part of the country is con-
cerned, was a train-load of some
600 students which last night was
making its way in fits and starts
along the Shanghai-Nanking Rail-
way in the direction of Nanking.

The train was commandeered
on Monday by the students, most-
ly from Fuh Tan University, at
North Station. On Tuesday even-
ing, the Railway authorities, act-
ing on the instructions of the City
Government, ran the train out
into the country, since the stu-
dents refused to leave it. At
Wusih the locomotive was de-
tached.

Locomotive Commandeered
Yesterday afternoon, according
to a long-distance telephone call
received by a local Chinese news-
paper, the students commandeered
another locomotive at Wusih,
attached it to their train, and
drove it themselves as far as
Changchow, thus bringing them
one station nearer to their goal.
They aim to reach Nanking and
there present demands to the Cen-
tral Government in regard to the
situation in North China.

Train services from North
Station were resumed yesterday,
but bookings on the Shanghai-
Nanking Railway were being
taken only as far as Soochow, be-
cause of the obstruction on the
line caused by the Fuh Tan stu-
dents and their train.

Since most would-be travellers
desired to go to Nanking and were
not prepared to take the chance
of being stranded en route, the
trains left North Station practi-
cally empty. Many persons desir-
ous of reaching the capital took
steamship passages, which, while
much slower, were considered
surpr. Many passengers Shang-
hai-bound from Nanking also
availed themselves of steamship
services.

A dinner was administered to
the student movement here on
Wednesday, when the authorities
closed all middle schools in Shang-
hai, except those usual for the
New Year Holiday, thereby de-
priving the students of their
customary meeting places. Many
of them will now be obliged to re-
turn to their homes.

Reason For Action
This action was taken on the
basis of an order by the Bureau
of Education "with a view to pre-
venting middle school students
from being exploited by Com-
munists and reactionary ele-
ments."

Dilating on the order, the
Bureau yesterday published the
following as an advertisement in
the local Chinese press:
"Students of middle schools,
being young, their intelligence is
not yet fully developed. Recent-
ly, a section of these students
have been instigated by undesir-
able elements to resort to illegal
activities. This Bureau has just
received an order from the Shang-
hai City Government instructing
that, for the protection of young
students, all public and private
middle schools in this locality
should commence the winter vaca-
tion at an earlier date.
"Principals of middle schools
are hereby notified to inform the
parents or guardians of students
to receive the students at their
homes at once in order to avoid
untoward incidents. Principals
of colleges and higher institutions
will be held responsible for the
observance of this order."

Citizens Support Students
Meanwhile, the Executive Com-
mittee of the First Special Dis-
trict Citizens' Federation has
taken a stand in connection with
the current patriotic movement
by passing the following resolu-
tions:
1.—That in view of the appeal
made by the local University
Students' National Salvation As-
sociation, preparations be made in
conjunction with other public
bodies to form a National Salva-
tion Association.
2.—That a petition be despatch-
ed to the National Government
requesting protection for all move-
ments aiming at the salvation of
the nation.
3.—That a warning be issued
to General Sung Cheh-yuan,
Chairman of the Chahar and
Hopei Political Council, to pre-
serve the territorial integrity and
sovereignty of China.

Kuomintang Acts
At the same time, the Shang-
hai Special District Kuomintang
has intervened in the situation to
prevent the student agitators
from being joined by the work-
ers organised in labour unions.
Summoning about 200 com-
mittee members of various unions
to the Tangpu office in Fengling-
chiao on Wednesday afternoon,
Mr. Loh Ching-m, a Kuomintang
official, directed them as follows:
1.—The committees of all labour
unions in Shanghai should explain
the students' movement to the
labourers.
2.—Particular attention should
be paid to ringleaders and their
movements should be reported when
discovered.
3.—All labourers should be
warned against being misled by
agitators.

THE CHINA PRESS, WEDNESDAY, DECEMBER 25, 1935

Fuh Tan Delegation At
North Station Takeu
Toward Nanking

RAILWAY PLANS TO
LEAVE THEM ON WAY

Forcible Ousting Was
Planned Here First,
Ruse Then Devised

For the stated purpose of
preventing communists and
students from exciting the
populace, General Wu Te-chen,
in the capacity as Mayor of
Greater Shanghai and Garri-
son Commander of the Shang-
hai Woosung Area, yesterday
at 8 p.m. declared martial law
in the following areas near
Shanghai: Yingziang, Kiang-
wan, Chapei, Pengpu and
Chenju.

City Government authorities,
after all measures had failed to
persuade some 2,500 students from
most of the leading Chinese uni-
versities and middle schools of the
city—500 of them girls—to leave
coaches most of them had occupied
at the North Station since 1 p.m.
Monday in an effort to get a free
ride to Nanking to demand imme-
diate military action against Japan,
10 coaches each took action yes-
terday.

At 5:05 and 5:15 p.m., engines
were coupled to two trains of 10
coaches each and left North Station
for Nanking, where a stop was to
be made to allow students to leave
for their homes in busses provided
for them. The trains were to
go on as far as Hsnil where the
students were to be ejected by force
and left to get back to Shanghai
as best they could.

Latest reports received here stated
that the two trains were still en
route.

Student Forces Augmented
Yesterday morning the Fuh Tan
students who remained since 1:30
p.m. on the preceding day, were
augmented by students from Great
China, Kwang Hwa, Tung Chi,
Chinan Universities, Chih Tse Col-
lege and several middle schools,
swelling the total ranks to 2,500,
some 500 of them girls and all of
them of the ages from 14 to 25.

At noon, Mayor Wu Te-chen held
a brief conference with university
school presidents at which it was
decided to ask the students once
more to leave the station, otherwise
they would be ejected by force at
3 p.m.

Dr. T. H. Li, President of Fuh Tan
University, Dr. J. Chang, Ex-Pre-
sident of Chinan University, and
other University presidents went to
the students at 1 p.m. to no avail.

At 2:30, a large contingent of
students headed by a banner reach-
ed the station and rushed to the
cars. They were joined by others
from fellow students. For some time,
reinforcements for the National
Preservation Corps, the Municipal
Police, and the Gendarmerie arrived.
The latter carried machine guns and
had them in place at the North
Station. Banners distributed sup-
plied to all students bore the
slogans of "Down with Japanese Im-
perialism" and "Save the Nation."

Station Like Armed Camp
At 3 p.m. the station looked like
an armed camp bristling with guns
carried by some 2,000 Paoantui and
policemen. Another attempt to
persuade the students was made,
but they continued adamant.

"You may threaten to behead us
yet we will go to Nanking," they
shouted. "You say we are commun-
ists: we are not." (Earlier in the
day some communists had distri-
buted literature. One of the student
leaders told a CHINA PRESS re-
porter that they did not allow com-
munistic students, who made at-
tempts, to join their ranks).

At 3:30, the police hung up sever-
al banners. They read: "Patriotic
students! Do not be misled by the
communists!" "Students! Don't let
yourselves be antagonized or provok-
ed." "Maintain order for the Stu-
dents' Patriotic Movement!"

At 4 p.m., Settlement police arriv-
ed on Boundary Road and attempt-
ed to disperse the thousands of on-
lookers with little success. The
Paoantui were all being armed with
bamboo poles and from that
time on the whole station was tense.

Suddenly at 4:05, the platform
loud speaker announced, "We have
received a telegram from Nanking.
The telegram states that you can
go to Nanking. Please board the
train quickly as the engines are due
very soon."

"It isn't true," one of the leaders
shouted. "Why are all the Paoantui
here? We will wait and see." In
the meanwhile, the Paoantui had
taken places on the platform, while
at the same time all the students,
crowded into two trains of 10 coaches
each. At 4:30 the loud speaker an-
nounced, "All students who wish to
leave now will be protected." Three
girls and one student left.

Shortly before 5 p.m., the Paoan-
tui were lining the two platforms
at which the trains were waiting.
Force seemed imminent and a last
attempt was made by a leader of
the Paoantui to persuade the stu-
dents to leave. The officer explain-
ed that the students were holding
up traffic and that they would be
protected if they left peacefully im-
mediately.

"If we are to be protected, why
are there thousands of Paoantui
here," a leader answered. "It pains
us to see this show of force. We
don't want the Paoantui."

"We are here to protect you," the
officer replied.

"We are peaceful. We don't need
your protection. We are determin-
ed to go to Nanking."

At this point, officials decided to
send the two trains on to Nanking,
where a halt would be made and
students would be asked to leave in
busses provided for them. A second
stop was made at Hsnil, where all
the remaining students were to be
forcibly ejected to make their way
back to Shanghai as best they could.
The trains left at 5:05 and 5:15 p.m.
respectively.

THE CHINA PRESS, WEDNESDAY, DECEMBER 25, 1935
Mayor Orders Martial Law As Activities Of Students Increase Here
Three Foreign Policemen, Five Students Hurt In Downtown Riot
March Of Students Into Settlement Culminates In Clash On Nanking Road; Japanese Consul-General Asks Suppression Of Movement

Three foreign officers of the Shanghai Municipal Police and five Chinese students were injured during a student riot staged in front of the Continental Emporium on Nanking Road about 9.30 a.m. yesterday.
The injured police officers are:
Sub-Inspector J. Furness.
Sergeant D. F. Watson.
Sergeant J. West.
Sub-Inspector Furness sustained a fractured arm when he was struck with a club, said to have been wielded by a student. Sergeant Watson received bruises and cuts about the face, while Sergeant West sustained lacerations on the forehead and cheek.
The incident was a development of a march into the Settlement by large groups of students and sympathizers from Chapel. Approximately 2,000 students, according to estimates made by the police, gathered on Nanking Road about 9.15 a.m. and shouting slogans, commenced the widespread distribution of pamphlets.
Groups of 200 and 300 entered the section from various streets. Some marched up from the Bund, others moved in from Chekiang and Honan Roads.
S. M. Police Called
Shouting of slogans and the distribution of pamphlets continued unhindered for about 10 minutes when police from Central and Louza Station and operatives of the Special Branch, S.M.P. began making arrests on the scene.
At first there was no disorder but students resented the police action and a scuffle ensued in which the three foreign officers were injured.
The students in the particular group where the trouble occurred were armed with sticks and clubs and used them freely against the police. Several students were arrested and taken to the Central Station.
One Group Marches West
One group of about 300 went west along Nanking Road to Bubbling Well Road, marched past the China United Apartments, the Foreign Y.M.C.A. and the Park Hotel. They continued to shout slogans as they marched, waving their hands at the same time. They paused for a moment near the Park Hotel, distributed pamphlets, and then turned north on Park Road and moved back across the Creek.
Five of the students were arrested near the Continental Emporium premises. Four of these had sustained slight injuries and two were taken to the First Special District Court shortly before noon and charge with assault and sentenced to three months imprisonment each, sentence suspended for two years.
No further trouble was reported in the International Settlement during the morning. About 1.30 p.m., however, a group of approximately 600 students and sympathizers marched through the Settlement, traveling south on Szechuen Road and going toward the French Concession. The procession was orderly but noisy, the minds of the marchers being largely occupied with the singing of slogans as they proceeded.
Along the Nanking Road section, however, over side-walks and in the road, thoroughfares were blocked yesterday afternoon by large crowds of students and sympathizers who had gathered to listen to speeches and to sing patriotic songs.

Ishii Asks Suppression
Assurances to curb anti-Japanese demonstrations and student activities in the International Settlement were given yesterday morning by Mr. Stirling Fessenden, Secretary-General of the Shanghai Municipal Council, to Mr. Itaro Ishii, Consul-General of Japan.
The Japanese official called at the S.M.C. at 10 o'clock, as police were still patrolling Nanking Road, after the early morning student demonstration.
Unable to arrange an interview with Gen. Wu Te-chen, Mayor of Greater Shanghai, Mr. Ishii telephoned a request to the latter for the immediate suppression of anti-Japanese activities.
The Japanese Embassy is "not considering" filing an official protest at this time in connection with the student demonstrations, a spokesman of the Embassy said last night.
The Japanese Naval Landing Party has taken no special precautions against eventualities, except for increasing the number of patrols. The parade of armored cars in the Hongkew district yesterday was described by a spokesman of the Landing Party as "maneuvers."
Special squads of the Japanese Consular Police, which began to patrol the streets of the Hongkew, Yangtszepoo and Irkadez districts yesterday, reported no arrests or incidents of any kind.
The local Japanese press took a calm view of the matter. The Shanghai Mainichi expressed the hope that the present student movement would not seriously affect Sino-Japanese relations. At the same time it warned the students that they should not be misled by agitators who seek to use them for their own ends.
It was generally believed that Communist agents were behind the present student movement. The Nippon Shimbun urged precautions to prevent the devil from disturbing the peace of the Far East under the guise of patriotism.

Seek An End For
'Autonomy' Regime

Chinese And Japanese
Negotiate In Peiping
Upon Issue

Sino-Japanese negotiations are being continued in Peiping for abolition of the "East Hopei Autonomous Government" in the demilitarized zone and the cessation of hostilities between Peace Preservation Corps and the "Manchukucan" troops along the Chahar border, Chinese reports from the former capital indicate.

General Sung Cheh-yuan, chairman of the Hopei-Chahar Political Council and "North China dictator" with five concurrent posts, is directing the negotiations while Major-General K. Doihara, the "Lawrence of Manchuria" is handling the parleys for the Japanese military authorities. The latter arrived in Peiping last night and was expected to call on General Sung today.

Ready For Compromise

As result of the preliminary discussions held in Peiping, Chinese authorities there are represented as optimistically expecting an early settlement of the Eastern Chahar dispute. Most fighting has been stopped along the Kuyuan-Paochang front although some sporadic clashes still are reported. The Japanese authorities are said to be ready to accept compromise plans for settlement of the disputes there.

Much doubt, however, is held concerning the Japanese attitude towards abolition of the "East Hopei Autonomous Government" established by Yin Ju-keng. Chinese authorities are understood to have promised cancellation of the National Government mandate ordering arrest and punishment of the rebels on condition that the "bogus government" be abolished. Reinstatement of Yin as commis-

sioner of the demilitarized zone is also said to have been promised.

Martial Law At Luantung

Martial law has been proclaimed by the "autonomous Government" in Luantung district as result of rumors that the Peace Preservation Corps, forming the "army" under Yin Ju-keng, are to declare severance of their connections with the "bogus organization." Units loyal to Yin have been rushed to various points to watch the movements.

Fresh "autonomy" uprisings, allegedly to be instigated by "ronin" in the Japanese Concession in Tientsin, were reported in the district of Wuan, Hopei, during the week-end. Hundreds of members of secret organizations attacked the city on Thursday. The magistrate, however, gallantly resisted. The attackers were finally repulsed when the authorities rushed reinforcements to the district. Ringleaders of the uprising escaped to Tientsin.

Student Demonstrations

Meanwhile, student demonstrations against the "autonomy" movement continued in various cities. In Shanghai, hundreds of young men and women paraded in the Settlement on Saturday evening. They were noisy but not disorderly. Last night, communist literature were distributed and handbills dropped from the roof garden of Sincere Company at Shanghai's "Time Square."

Three thousand students paraded in Taiyuan, Shansi, yesterday while in Hankow, more than 2000 students of Wuchang crossed the river to parade on the streets. More will participate in another parade today. In Paotingfu, 600 students paraded. More than 1000 paraded in Yangchow, Kiangsu.

Two Resign

The demonstrations have resulted in resignation of two officials. Dr. Chu Ching-nen, commissioner of Education of the Hunan Provincial Government, has submitted his resignation for having failed to prevent the student demonstrations while in Hangchow. Dr. Z. Y. Kwok, president of the National

University of Chekiang, resigned over disputes arising from the student movements.

In Shanghai, students are resuming their classes as usual and National Salvation Associations formed.

The Peiping Student Union, according to the Sin Wen Pao, held a conference on Saturday and turned down the proposals to stage a third demonstration and to advance the winter recess.

THE CHINA WEEKLY REVIEW
December 21, 1935

Temporary Settlement of the North China Crisis
BY T. S. YOUNG

GEN. HO YING-CHIN, Minister of War, must be congratulated on his success in cracking a very hard nut. While the formula, by which the tense situation prevailing in North China may be temporarily liquidated, may not be totally satisfactory to many of our people who have grieved at the further loss of our national prestige and position, it, nevertheless, must be considered as the best arrangement which Gen. Ho can make in face of the Japanese determination to detach five northern provinces from the jurisdiction of the Chinese Government. So long as China is not in a position to resort to arms to defend her territorial integrity, she has no alternative but to seek a modus operandi at great pains to accommodate Japanese wishes and meet Japanese demands. The present arrangement in instituting a separate political council for governing Hopei and Chahar provinces seems to be acceptable to all the parties concerned: China has saved her important "face" by retaining the nominal control over this political council; Japan has firmly established her authority over North China; and many of the remnants of the old Peking Government have got their jobs and their forgotten names once again to the public notice.

China has indeed saved her "face." Inasmuch as the members of this Hopei-Chahar Political Council have been appointed by the Chinese Government, Nanking, on the surface, has retained its authority over these two northern provinces. At one time, the situation appeared so hopeless, that only a miracle could thwart the Japanese determination in carrying out to its successful conclusion the so-called North China Autonomous Movement. Through protracted negotiations and painstaking efforts, Gen. Ho eventually worked out a formula, by which a separate political council composed of as many as seventeen members would be formed to govern Hopei and Chahar provinces. How far and how long Nanking can retain its nominal authority over this political council, can not be told; but in comparison with what the Japanese militarists had originally planned to carry out, the present arrangement is decidedly the lesser of two evils. In view of the high military pressure exerted by the Japanese Kwantung Army and the questionable loyalty of a few of leading northern officials, we must not blame the responsible authorities of the Central Government for their failure in making a better settlement of this crisis. To all intents and purposes, the Chinese Government has really done all it can in making the best of a very bad bargain.

Japan Consolidates Her Position in North China

Japan has definitely consolidated her position in North China as a result of new political developments. Without firing a single shot, she has succeeded in creating a political hegemony in Hopei and Chahar. For the time being, the warlords of the Japanese Kwantung Army may be satisfied with their new gains, but it can not be expected that they will contentedly give up their long cherished objective of alienating North China from Nanking. By all means, the present political set-up is merely a makeshift, and how long it will last will all depend upon the whims of the Japanese warlords. When the opportune time comes, they can easily find a new pretence to force new terms upon the Chinese officials. Therefore it will not surprise us if the present Hopei-Chahar Political Council might become a North China Political Council before long. Perhaps the Japanese warlords have preferred this gradual process of disintegrating China, because it will arouse less opposition from the world, and therefore be more sure of its successful consummation.

This new political set-up has incidentally created many jobs for the jobless retired politicians, who have long connived with the Japanese intriguers in promoting any separatist movements with the hope of regaining their political position and fortune. Wang I-tang and Kao Lin-wei, two members of the newly constituted Council, are the leading members of the notorious Anfu clique, which has had many unsavory misdeeds to its credit in the days of the old Peking Government. During the present crisis, many names of the members of that clique have been frequently mentioned as accomplices of Japanese promoters of the autonomous movement. It is hoped that the generosity shown by the Central Government toward these trouble makers will in some way wake up their conscience, so that henceforth in serving the new Council, they will refrain themselves from either instigating or participating in any anti-government activities, and exemplify their loyalty to the country.

The most interesting personality of the new Council is its Chairman, Gen. Sung Cheh-yuen. Gen. Sung, a former subordinate of Gen. Feng Yu-hsiang, achieved quite a big fame for his being able to put up a stiff resistance against the Japanese invaders along the Great Wall in the Spring of 1933. As the Chairman of Chahar province, he was frequently stigmatized by the Japanese as a "bandit" leader, and was forced to quit that office under the Japanese pressure last July. While the Japanese attacks against him had not yet died down, he, all of a sudden and to the surprise of all, was accepted by the Kwantung Army as a persona grata, and possibly on the Japanese request, was appointed as the Garrison Commander of the Peiping-Tientsin area. Since then he has virtually held the key position of North China. His present appointment as the Chairman of the Council has been expected, but the fact that a "bandit" leader can suddenly become a favorite of the Japanese warlords remains a mystery.

To Gen. Ho must be given the credit of temporarily liquidating the North China crisis. But without belittling the importance of Gen. Ho's work, it must be admitted that his eloquence and ability alone could not change the adamant attitude of the Japanese warlords. Unexpectedly and to the discomfiture of Japanese warlords, this autonomous movement in North China caused such a consternation to the world, that both Cordell Hull, Secretary of State of the U.S. Government, and Sir Samuel Hoare, Foreign Secretary of the British Government, simultaneously made public statements regarding the North China situation to remind Japan of the fact that the western world was not preoccupied with Italo-Ethiopian case. In their statements, neither Secretary Hull nor Sir Samuel disguised their belief that Japanese figures were playing an active part in the autonomous movement. It is more than a coincidence that Secretary Hull and Sir Samuel should comment on the North China situation at the same time. No matter how strong minded the Japanese warlords are reputed to be, they can not ignore the warnings given by the two leading Powers of the world. In face of the concerted action on the part of the United States and Britain, the Japanese warlords had to trim their sails and give an ear to Gen. Ho's overtures.

One Rule for Manchuria—Another for Ethiopia

The League of Nations has already been subject to severe criticisms, for it has two sets of rules—one for the Manchurian Affairs and another for the Ethiopian case. It has always been asked that if sanctions can be applied against Italy now, why should they not have been applied against Japan about four years ago? Japan must consider herself very fortunate in having such a very narrow escape from this economic weapon wielded by the world's peace machinery. But who can tell that the League will not reopen the case in the light of present Japanese aggressions by applying sanctions against Japan at present? The new Foreign Secretary of the British Government is quite a different man from his predecessor, and has already been praised for his diplomatic skill and ability. In view of the fact that a strong man is now directing the British foreign policy, and that the League of Nations, for the first time of its history, has applied economic sanctions against Italy, Japan, with her guilty conscience, can not but reconsider her determined stand in realizing her wide dreams.

Dr. C. T. Wang's recent trip to Japan and his exchange of opinions with the leading officials of the Japanese Government might also lend some weight to the settlement of the North China crisis. That Dr. Wang should take a sudden trip to Japan and seek interviews with Japanese officials at the very time when the situation in North China was very tense can not be said as being for the purpose of seeking personal pleasure and renewing acquaintance with his friends only. What was his mission will, of course, remain a matter of conjecture, but it is not unreasonable to suggest that he was sent by the Central Government to Japan for the purpose of explaining China's definite stand vis-a-vis the so-called North China Autonomous Movement. It may be also presumed that as a result of his visit, the Japanese Government has sent Col. Seiichi Kita, Chief of the China Section of the Japanese General-Staff, to China to bring new instructions to the warlords of the Kwantung Army.

With the temporary settlement of the North China crisis, our people can now heave a sigh of great relief. But it must be remembered that the political horizon over North China is far from being clear and bright, and unexpected developments may happen any time. Col. Kita was quoted as having said that future developments, subsequent to the establishment of the Hopei-Chahar Political Council, will be "much more important than what has taken place so far." He further said, "Since North China events must seriously affect the future relations between Japan, Manchukuo and China, we shall have to keep a close watch over the situation until it comes to a complete settlement." Suffice it to say that the Japanese warlords will not consider the complete settlement of the North China situation, until the five northern provinces have severed their connection with Nanking and come totally under the Japanese control.

Peiping Students Stage Demonstration
Against Autonomy Move

Opposing any attempt to establish any "autonomous government" in North China, more than 4000 students in Peiping made a demonstration on December 9. They walked out from their campuses and schools, and proceeded in long parade, defying armed policemen and gendarmes. Minor clashes occurred at Morrison Street and the Kao Liang Bridge, resulting in the injury of several students and the arrest of about 20 students of the North-eastern University. On the next and following days, a "peace strike" was launched in the many universities and schools, "until the following demands would be complied with":

"That the students arrested in the demonstration be released immediately; that the medical care fee of the injured demonstrators be compensated by the Peiping Municipal Government; that the policemen responsible for the injuring of the demonstrators be consistently punished; and that any special political organization in North China be not set up."

The staging of the demonstration followed a motion passed by the newly-founded Peiping Students' Association, which had been initiated by the student bodies of two middle schools, and included the student bodies of Yenching and Tsinghua Universities. According to the Association's plan, the demonstrators were to assemble as destination in front of the Hsin Hua Men, where they attempted to see General Ho Ying-chin, who had recently been called up to deal with the situation. The closing of the city-gates, however, compelled the demonstrators to be divided into two groups. One group of about 1000 students, mostly from Yenching and Tsinghua Universities, demonstrated outside the city, while the other paraded inside.

Early in the morning, when the weather was bitterly cold, Yenching and Tsinghua students started from their respective campuses, situated about five miles to the west of Peiping, and proceeded on foot to the city, for the bus-services were suspended under police orders. After having failed several times to halt the progress of the parade, the police reinforced their strength on the Kao Liang Bridge where an army of Sung T'ai-tsung had ever fought fiercely against Chi Tang, a Manchurian race. But the students broke asunder their array and rushed forward to the gate where they stubbornly waited, returning at four in the afternoon.

On the other hand, several hundred students from other universities, colleges, and middle schools inside the city gathered in front of the Hsin Hua Men, shouting anti-"autonomy" slogans and waving banners bearing similar sentiments. Hou Cheng, secretary to General Ho Ying-chin, suggested to them that as Gen. Ho had gone to the Tangshan Hot Spring, he would transmit the sentiments of the students to him. The students, however, did not agree. It was later confirmed that General Ho was actually still staying in the city. They paraded throughout the city, stopping at many schools and universities calling for more students to join the demonstration, until the number increased to two thousand. Entering Morrison Street the enthusiasm of the demonstrators were dampened by fire hoses, maneuvered by the police. Clashes occurred when the leaders tried to seize the fire hoses resulting in the injury of several students, among whom was a girl student, who was thrust in her breasts with a bayonet by a policeman.

Prior to the demonstration, the student bodies of National Peking and Tsinghua Universities, following the lead of their respective deans and chancellors, had previously issued statements, repudiating the suggestion that the camouflaged autonomous movement had popular support. A joint declaration among the many students bodies, initiated by the Yenching student body, resolved on four points: "That we are resolutely opposed to the so-called 'anti-communist self-governing' and call for the punishment of Yin Ju-keng; that we call for the Central Government to make public its foreign policy; that we call for the Central Government to mobilize the whole nation to resist our enemy; and that we claim the liberty of the press and the holding of meetings."
W.C.J.

Students in South China Agitate Against
Japanese
(By cable from the Review's South China Correspondent)

CANTON, December 16.—Despite the verbal protest of the Japanese Consul-General here to the Municipal Government, the student movement continues to develop in intensity with cries for the revival of anti-Japanese agitation, including the anti-Japanese boycott, loudly voiced. Thirty senior colleges have joined students from Chungshan University in their demonstrations and held a large mass-meeting yesterday.

The assurances and cautions of the officials have not prevented students from organizing a picket corps whose intention it is to visit all Chinese shops and to seize Japanese goods.

The Chinese officials here are obviously worried, fearing international complications. Consequently, General Chen Chi-tang has summoned Chunshan professors personally instructing them to cease the boycott agitation and to advise the students to discontinue their one-week strike.

On December 12, 2,000 students, led by Chang Nung, dean of Agriculture, and other faculty members from Chungshan University, held a militant demonstration and street parade in which huge flamboyant banners were carried. Handbills were distributed everywhere protesting the Japanese-engineered autonomy moves in North China. Chinese teachers educated in Japan participated in the demonstration as the chief organizers. The demonstrators wired to Nanking demanding the release of 27 students held in Peiping, the suppression of the autonomists in North China, the restoration of the freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, and freedom of publication, and the cessation of the negotiation of secret treaties with Japan.

Students in Shanghai, Peiping and Tientsin Pro-
test Against "Autonomous" Government

A meeting of students in which all local universities and colleges were represented was held in Shanghai Dec. 15 when a resolution was unanimously adopted to oppose the formation of any semblance of an autonomous regime in North China and to advocate that the severest of punishment be meted out to Yin Ju-keng and other "autonomist" ringleaders in the North. It was, however, agreed that this stand of the students should be presented to the government and public through legitimate channels without recourse to class strikes or indignation demonstrations, which have been frowned upon by both school and Chinese government authorities.

Students of the Peiping Normal University Dec. 15 sent a lengthy telegram to the Governments and peoples of all nations voicing strong opposition to the so-called autonomy movement in North China. The Tientsin Students' Association issued a declaration on the same date in support of the demands made by the Peiping students.

Shanghai "Nippo" Blames American Influence
for Student Movement in China

Commenting on the wide-spread movement of students and cultural organizations in Peiping, Canton, and Shanghai, against autonomy and against Japan, the Shanghai Nippo alleges that, behind the scenes of the student movement, which is gaining strength throughout the country, someone is pulling the wires. "For instance," the paper continues, "the bulk of students who engaged in the recent demonstrations in Peiping against autonomy, were students of missionary schools. Moreover, the student movement has been carried out under the leadership of professors who are graduates of American universities. It is almost indisputable that the students are only the prey of propaganda by the politicians, including Chang Ya-kwang, one of the leaders of Peiping People's Anti-Japanese League, and Hsia Chang-kwang, a representative of the anti-Japanese Volunteers in the North East, both of whom went from the North to Canton via Shanghai." The paper further argues that since at present the students are still the leading representatives of Chinese intellectuals, just as they were ten years ago, this is vivid proof that the cultural development of China has lagged.

"Sin Wen Pao" Denounces Interference With Students

In an editorial Dec. 13 the Sin Wen Pao, leading Chinese daily journal in Shanghai, in strong words denounced the actions of the Chinese authorities in North China in arresting students who participated in the demonstration on December 9 and in taking special precautions, such as guarding Peiping school entrances with soldiers.

"What crime have the students of Peiping committed, that they deserve detention? Is their patriotic movement a crime? How is it that with the exception of the students in Peiping, there are no patriotic citizens in China? How is it that the authorities use the soldiers to prevent the students carrying out any patriotic movement instead of fighting against the aggressors?" the paper queried.

MAYOR WU'S ADVICE
TO THE STUDENTS

Commends Demonstrator
Orderliness, Advises
Self-Restraint

A statement in the form of a public letter to local students was issued last night by Mayor Wu Te-chen in which he expressed his appreciation of the orderly manner in which the student demonstrations were conducted, but at the same time declared that he felt much concerned. The Mayor emphasized that the national crisis, which was the chief source of the students' worry, had evolved from historical events and that to tide over the crisis "perpetual endeavour" instead of free play of the emotions was the correct policy.

The Central Government had a fixed foreign policy and paid serious attention to the territorial and administrative rights of the country. It would not shirk its responsibility. Hence those rights and interests which must belong to a nation would be protected, Mayor Wu said. Because of the weakness of the people, the authorities had not so far been able to solve the problem to the fullest extent and it was the duty of the people to co-operate with the Government so that it could adopt a more effective policy.

Mayor Wu pointed out that the weakness of the student movements in the past was that the youths often could not distinguish the means from the end, and this enabled reactionary elements to make use of the situation. Concluding, the Mayor asked the students to focus their attention on studies, quoting a German philosopher as saying that today's war was a war of character, morality and intelligence.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, THURSDAY, DECEMBER 12, 1935

Kuyuan Now In Hands Of
Manchoukuo Troops, Say
Peiping Chinese Reports

General Doihara Said To Have Offered To Mediate
On Condition Mongol Police Are Sent
To The Frontier Posts

SEIZURE OF BOTH CUSTOMS AND SALT
REVENUE ORDERED BY YIN

PEIPING, Dec. 11.—The town of Kuyuan, a few miles inside the Chahar border, which was besieged by Manchoukuo troops from Jehol on Monday, is now in the hands of the attackers, according to reliable Chinese sources here. No details are available except that the local Chinese Peace Preservation Corps retreated from Kuyuan after their commander, Li Keh-cheng, had succumbed to wounds received in action. Twelve of his men were also wounded and were subsequently removed to Changpei for treatment. Apparently no further fighting occurred after the initial engagement, the Manchoukuo troops occupying the town on the retreat of the defenders.

Because of the remoteness of Kuyuan from ordinary means of communication, the exact situation here is still obscure, even the Japanese military spokesman here stating to-day that he had no news. A Chinese report which cannot yet be confirmed states that Major-General Doihara, of the Kwantung Army has offered to mediate for a settlement of the “Kuyuan affair” on condition that the Chinese authorities agree to station Mongol peace preservation men both there and at Paochang if the Manchoukuo troops now in occupation withdraw.—Reuter

Students Stop Work
PEIPING, Dec. 11.—Further demonstrations against the so-called autonomy movement are likely to be witnessed here if plans now being discussed by the student leaders materialise. The main object will be to secure the release of students arrested on Monday and still held in custody.

Anxious to prevent further disorders, the military authorities today placed “Big Sword” and pistol squad at the entrances to the various Government and private Universities here.

Although no formal strike has been declared, class-work at five Universities is at a standstill. Students are absenting themselves from their class-rooms at Yenching, Tsing Hua, the National University, the Peking National University and the Peiping National Normal University.

The Chancellors of the these five institutions met at mid-day today to discuss the situation, but their decisions have not been disclosed.

A curious situation prevails at Yenching, where the student organisation appears to be split as can that of the other Universities here.

Customs Seizure Ordered
PEIPING, Dec. 11.—It is reported to-day from Tungchow, seat of the rebel regime in East Hopei, that Mr. Yin Ju-keng, head of the “Autonomous Council,” has ordered the magistrates of the 22 hsien in the Demilitarized Zone to detain all Customs and Salt revenue in the areas under their jurisdiction.

This means interference with the Customs at all passes along the Great Wall, as well as at Shanhaikwan, Chingwangtao and Tangshan.

Mr. Yin is also said to have prohibited the circulation in the Demilitarised Zone of notes of the Central Bank of China and of all Chinese banks in Shanghai, while he is reported to have issued orders to the Salt Commissioner at Changlu to hand over all revenue to his Revenue Bureau in Tangshan.—Reuter.

The New Council
NANKING, Dec. 11.—Arrangements have been completed concerning the personnel and organization of the proposed “Hopei and Chahar Political Council,” and an announcement, in the form of a Government mandate, is now expected to be made to-morrow.

Meanwhile, General Shang Chen, who appears determined to resign the Governorship of Hopei, is being mentioned as Chairman of Honan in succession to General Liu Shih, who is likely to become Pacification Commissioner for Honan and Anhwei.

In any case it appears certain that General Shang Chen will be given an important appointment outside Hopei.

It is reported that General Hsiao Chen-yin, Governor of Chahar, will succeed Mr. Cheng Keh as the Mayor of Tientsin, while General Chang Chih-chung, at present acting Chairman of Chahar, will receive a substantive post.—Reuter.

New Aerodrome In Tientsin
NANKING, Dec. 11.—Both the Military Affairs Commission and the Executive Yuan have received reports from the military authorities in Peiping concerning the construction of a Japanese aerodrome in Tientsin.

Construction of the airfield in Tientsin has been pushed forward in disregard of protest from local Chinese authorities, the reports state.

The Central authorities, it is reliably learnt, are considering appropriate steps to deal with the problem.—Central News.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, FRIDAY, DECEMBER 6, 1935

General Sung Cheh-yuan
Causes Flurry By Sudden
Departure For Tientsin

Written Statement Interpreted In Chinese Circles
To Indicate That He Will No Longer Assume
Full Responsibility For Peiping

GENERAL HO YING-CHIN CONFERS WITH
LEADING MILITARY COMMANDERS

PEIPING; Dec. 5.—A flurry was caused in local Chinese circles to-day by the sudden, unexpected departure from the ancient capital of General Sung Cheh-yuan, Garrison Commander of Peiping and Tientsin, whose exit cast a damper on the optimism prevailing here that the crisis in North China would soon be composed.

General Sung was at first reported to have gone to a villa in the Western Hills, near Peiping, but this appears to have been a blind, for it was reliably reported this evening that he had arrived at Tientsin. General Sung, who has a house in the British Concession there, is stated to have made the journey by road and to have arrived at his destination this afternoon.

A written statement issued this afternoon by General Sung is interpreted in Chinese circles as indicating that he will no longer assume full responsibility for the maintenance of peace and order in Peiping.

Confidence In Ho

The statement declares that the situation in North China has greatly improved since the arrival of General Ho, and that he is confident that the Chinese War Minister will be able to find a solution.

General Sung refers to his task, as commandant of the Peiping and Tientsin garrisons, of maintaining peace and order, and adds:

"Now that General Ho Ying-chin has come to Peiping, I feel that my work has been considerably lightened. Henceforth, I will deal with all difficult problems in accordance with instructions from General Ho."

The craft circled above the "Chü Jen-tang" hall, the temporary residence of General Ho Yin-chin, Chinese Minister of War, who arrived here on Tuesday empowered by the Nanking Government to take whatever measures he should find necessary to settle the North China situation.—Rengo.

Palace Museum Treasures

PEIPING, Dec. 3.—According to Chinese reports, the Palace Museum is sending shortly 500 cases of art treasures to Nanking and Shanghai.

The decision to ship the treasures from Peiping was made after the return of Mr. Chang Ting-chi, Director of the Department of General of the Museum, from Shanghai last week.

The Curio Museum is also arranging to remove its art treasures to Nanking. This Museum is under the control of the Ministry of the Interior in Nanking, while the Palace Museum is under the Executive Yuan direct.—Reuter.

PEIPING, Dec. 5.—"I am well and safe," declared Mr. Yin Ju-keng, head of the so-called Autonomous State of East Hopei, when told of a report widely circulated in China yesterday that he had been assassinated.

Mr. Yin readily came to the telephone when inquirers rang up his headquarters at Tungchow, in the Demilitarized Zone, from Peiping.

He added that all was quiet in Tungchow, and that he was proceeding steadily with his arrangements for the administration of the new "State."—Reuter.

Aerial Demonstrations

PEIPING, Dec. 5.—The Japanese are subjecting Peiping to thorough aerial demonstrations. Aeroplanes circled over the headquarters of General Ho Yin-chin yesterday, while to-day 14 Japanese machines, as well as a plane belonging to the so-called Autonomous Government of East Hopei, visited the ancient capital.

The "East Hopei," a plane which formerly belonged to the Japanese and which was piloted by a Japanese, flew over the city at one o'clock this afternoon, dropping thousands of leaflets which called for support of the "autonomous scheme" and offered congratulations to the East Hopei Council on their inauguration.

Then, at 2.30 p.m., five planes flying in formation roared low over the city, being followed an hour later by nine planes, which also flew in formation.

The planes were obviously not reconnoitring, but were purely for purposes of demonstration. Their origin is unknown, but as they came out from the North, it is probable that they were from Jehol.

Tsao Kun In Tientsin

TIENTSIN, Dec. 5.—Contrary to current reports, General Tsao Kun, former leader of the Chihli clique, has not gone to Peiping, but is still in Tientsin, confining himself to his residence in the British Concession here and amusing himself with Chinese painting. Except with General Wu Pei-fu, with whom he is in frequent communication, it is understood that General Tsao has refused to receive all his other former followers.—Chekiai.

Refugees In Tangshan

TIENTSIN, Dec. 5.—In view of the troublous situation in the East Hopei following the establishment of the so-called Autonomous Government by Yin Ju-keng, most of the well-to-do inhabitants there have left their homes to seek refuge in Tangshan. Owing to the sudden increase of population, it is learned that all the vacant unoccupied houses in Tangshan have been filled to overflowing.—Chekiai.

LONDON, Dec. 5.—Disturbances among Hopei peasants following the autonomous movement in the province were reported here today. It is said that many villages have been looted by the bandits operating in the area.

IMPARTIAL NOT NEUTRAL

A RÉSUMÉ

Events in North China find their origin in the absorption of Jehol by Manchoukuo with the support of Japanese troops early in 1934 and the subsequent signature of the Tangku Truce on May 31, of that year. That agreement created the demilitarized zone—an area of 5,000 square miles between the Great Wall and a line running from Yenching to Lutai. It was accompanied by certain verbal undertakings given by the Chinese signatories to the Japanese. On the basis of those undisclosed terms negotiations between the Japanese military authorities and the Chinese administration in the North have, from time to time, been conducted. The tenor of each pronouncement on such negotiations has established the fact that a wide freedom of interpretation has been consistently reserved by the Japanese, so that in handling affairs in the North the Chinese authorities have been compelled to follow Japanese dictation which has developed an appetite by the mere process of feeding. On May of this year this journal's Peiping correspondent reported a sudden turn in the course of events in the presentation to General Ho Ying-chin, the Chairman of the Peiping Military Council (and War Minister in the National Government) of certain demands from the Kwantung Army. These demands were indicated by the subsequent removal of the headquarters of the Hopei Provincial Government from Tientsin to Paotingfu, the elimination from the Peiping Military Council of elements declared to be unsatisfactory to the Japanese, the closing of the local Kuomintang offices, and the withdrawal—carried out with lightning speed—of General Yu Hsueh-chang's troops and the resignation of the General himself from the charge of the Hopei Government. The activities of Sun Yung-chin at the head of so-called Chinese volunteers in the demilitarized zone and the murder of two Japanophile Chinese editors in the Japanese Concession in Tientsin were the ostensible causes of this action by the Kwantung Army. Early in June the removal of General Sung Cheh-yuan from the Governorship of Charhar, together with all his troops, was also demanded. General Ho Ying-chin was pressed to give a written acceptance of the Japanese demands but he declined and reported to the Government at Nanking on June 12.

On June 18 it was announced that the Government had replaced General Sung Cheh-yuan in the Governorship of Charhar by General Chin Teh-chung and had appointed Mr. Wang Keh-min to be acting Chairman of the Peiping Military Council in place of General Huang Fu who had held that appointment since May 1934 and had retired owing to ill-health. Meanwhile the Kwantung Army announced that General Sung Cheh-yuan and his troops, having broken the Tangku Truce would be regarded as bandits. On June 27, Major-General Kenji Doihara secured the written agreement of General Chin Teh-chung to a settlement of the Charhar dispute, including reparation for the arrest of four civilian employees of the Kwantung Army at Changpei on June 5. Rumours of a separatist movement were current and on June 28 some insurgents—among whom were Japanese "ronin" subsequently deported to Japan—seized an armoured train and with it launched an attack on Peiping. The attempt was quickly suppressed by the local Chinese authorities. A lull in the situation then followed until on August 4 the murder of Colonel Liu Tso-chiu of the Peace Preservation Corps and the wounding of Japanese gendarme by Chinese assailants prompted an urgent representation by the Japanese military authorities to Mr. Wang Keh-min, the conversation including a suggestion that the five northern provinces should be reorganized. Mr. Tao Shang-min, an inspector of the demilitarized zone was detained at the Japanese Embassy on August 6 and not released until August 17. after a protest by the Government at Nanking. On August 28, General

Sung Cheh-Yuan, having apparently lost his "bandit" status on the Japanese books, was appointed Garrison Commander of the Peiping-Tientsin area with enhanced powers. The Government also decided on the same day to abolish the Peiping Political Council — a decision which took effect on September 1, thus terminating the two years' existence of a sorely-tried organization. On September 2 to General Shang Chen who, as persona grata to the Japanese, had been appointed to succeed General Yu Hsueh-chang as Chairman of the Hopei Government in June, the Japanese Consul-General at Tientsin reiterated the demand for the suppression of terrorist organizations in Hopei and accused the provincial authorities of negligence in that regard. On September 25 disclosure of a Japanese military memorandum —attributed to the staff of General Tada—outlined a definite scheme of autonomy for the Northern provinces of China. Political and economic collaboration between China, Japan and Manchoukuo was commended by an official announcement at Tokyo toward the end of September. On October 18, Mr. Akira Ariyoshi in an interview with this journal referred to the situation in the North as "not unsatisfactory," but affirmed Japan's policy of regarding the Government at Nanking as the Central Government of China. PAOTING CONFERENCE
OPENS AT NIGHT
