THE SHANGHAI TIMES, TUESDAY, DECEMBER 3, 1935
War Minister Arrives
In Paotingfu; Enters
Into Parleys At Once
Formation Of Northern Political Council Having
Control Over Five Provinces Discussed In
Well-Informed Circles In Peiping
JAPANESE MILITARY IMPATIENT OVER
CONTINUED UNSETTLED CONDITIONS
PEIPING, Dec. 2.—The one question being asked here
to-day is whether General Ho Ying-chin, the Chinese War
Minister, who has been sent to Peiping by the Nanking
Government as Resident Representative of the Executive
Yuan, will be able to save the five Northern Provinces, or
part of them, for China. It is felt that he has a fairly good
chance of organizing a form of semi-independent adminis-
tration which will go a long way towards meeting Japanese
requirements, while remaining nominally under the control
of Nanking. Well-informed Chinese are discussing the
possibility of the formation of a body to be known as the
Northern Political Council of the Republic of China, which
would control the provinces of Hopei, Shantung, Shansi,
Chahar and Suiyuan.
It is suggested that this Coun-
cil be a fairly large body of per-
haps 40 members, including a
number of retired Northern milit-
arists and officials residing in
this area, but that unquestionably,
General Sung Cheh-yuan, Garrison
Commander of Peiping and
Tientsin, must head the Council,
as he is the only man in this
area with sufficient troops to
maintain peace and order. The
status of the new body would be
similar to that of the Mongol
Autonomous Council.
The plan, it is believed, might
be accepted by the Japanese.
Major-General Doihara, of the
Kwantung Army, is understood
to have already discussed with
General Sung Cheh-yuan, and to
have indicated his readiness to
discuss it further. It is evident,
however, that settlement of
North China's affairs brooks of
no delays.
The Japanese military spokes-
man indicated to-day the growing
impatience of the Japanese milit-
ary authorities over the unsettled
conditions of North China.
Asked about the autonomy
movement, he said that it was
"still progressing, but no im-
mediate developments were to be
expected." If General Ho Ying-
chin came to Peiping, he added,
no negotiations would be carried
on with him, although he might
visit the Japanese authorities.
Autonomy, he added, would come
first, and then afterwards there
might be a discussion of an ad-
ministration and council for this
area.
Peiping Mayor's Wire
General Chin Teh-chun, the
Mayor of Peiping, to-day tele-
graphed to the Nanking authori-
ties urging them to devise
measures to deal with the situa-
tion in North China.
It is felt that this action by
General Chin, together with the
recent statements made by Mr.
Ching Keh, Mayor of Tientsin,
and General Sung Cheh-yuan,
pave the way for the declaration
of autonomy, while they fear they
will inevitably be forced to make.
Major-General Doihara, accord-
ing to a high Chinese official, has
intimated to General Sung that
further delay in satisfying the
situation and the autonomist
demands will be difficult.
General Sung is reported to
have replied that, as long as the
demonstrations are orderly, the
authorities will not interfere with
them.
General Sung and other officials
are going to Paotingfu, the Hopei
provincial capital, to meet Gen-
eral Ho Ying-chin, who arrives
there to-day.
It is expected that they will
confer with General Shang Chen,
Governor of Hopei, but whether
General Ho will come to Peiping
after all is doubtful in view of
his reported statement at Hsu-
chow: He is said to have express-
ed uncertainty whether he would
assume his new post at Peiping.
Questioned to-day concerning
the reported arrival at Shan-
haikwan of ten Japanese troop
trains from Mukden, the Japan-
ese military spokesmen declared
that he had no information con-
cerning the matter.
Persistent reports that three
divisions of troops are being sent
from Japan to North China are
discredited in all well-informed
quarters here.—Reuter.
Autonomy Committee
NANKING, Dec. 2.—Well-in-
formed circles here state that
General Sung Cheh-yuan, Garri-
son Commander of Peiping and
Tientsin, has suggested the est-
ablishment of a Hopei Anti-Red
Autonomy Committee with him-
self as Chairman.
It is further stated that this
suggestion will be discussed by
General Ho Ying-chin, Minister
of War, and General Sung.—
Reuter.
General Cheng Yi
TIENTSIN, Dec. 2.—General
Cheng Yi, Governor of Fukien,
who arrived here this morning
from Nanking, will leave to-night
for Peiping.
He refused to grant any inter-
views, but his departure for
Peiping is regarded as indicat-
ing that the establish-
ment of the new regime in
North China is imminent.
It is believed here that General
Ho, who is en route to Paotingfu,
will remain there until he hears
from General Cheng Yi before
leaving for Peiping.
Mr. Ching Keh, the Mayor of
Tientsin, signalized his return
from Peiping to-day by despatch-
ing a number of telegrams urging
that the Chinese Government take
the initiative in establishing an
autonomous regime in North
China in order to preserve China's
sovereign rights.
The director and representatives
of the nine autonomy districts in
Tientsin have telegraphed to Nan-
king urging the Central Govern-
ment to take effective measures
for the safety of Hopei, and de-
claring that district autonomy
was the best solution for the pres-
ent difficulties. A similar tele-
gram was despatched by the Chin-
ese Chamber of Commerce.—
Reuter.
Uncertain Whether To Assume Post
NANKING, Dec. 2.—Interview-
ed when he passed through Hsu-
chow yesterday, General Ho Ying-
chin is reported to have told
pressmen that he was uncertain
whether he would assume his new
post at Peiping.—Reuter.
Dr. Wang Calls On Hirota
TOKYO, Dec. 2.—Dr. C. T.
Wang, formerly Minister for For-
eign Affairs at Nanking, called
at the Foreign Office this morn-
ing and had an interview with Mr.
Hirota, the Japanese Minister for
Foreign Affairs, and Mr. Shige-
mitsu, the Vice-Minister.
Discussing the Sino-Japanese
situation at his daily conference
with pressmen, the spokesman of
the Foreign Office said Japan con-
sidered that the departure of Gen-
eral Ho Ying-chin for North
China signified that General
Chiang Kai-shek did not want to
discuss affairs there with the
Japanese Ambassador, Mr. Ariyo-
shi.—Reuter.
Two Japanese Said Killed
PEIPING, Dec. 2.—An incident
alleged to have cost the lives of
two Japanese is reported from
Tawangchang, a village situated
east of Tientsin.
The two Japanese are said to
have gathered the villagers to-
gether on Saturday and to have
harangued them on the subject of
autonomy.
The audience, so the story goes,
manhandled the Japanese, who are
reported to have been fatally
wounded.
The report is confirmed in
semi-official sources, but the
Japanese authorities and the vari-
ous newspapers in North China
are silent on the subject.—
Reuter.
A Call On General Tada
TIENTSIN, Dec. 2.—Arriving
here from the capital, obviously
to seek an understanding with the
Japanese military authorities on
the North China visit of General
Ho Ying-chin, Chinese Minister of
War, two Nanking emissaries this
morning were accorded an
interview by General Hayao Tada,
commander of the Nippon forces
in North China.
General Chen I, Chairman of the
Fukien Provincial Government,
and Mr. Yin Tung, former man-
aging director of the Peiping-
Liaoning Railway, arrived here at
8 o'clock this morning. The latter
called alone at General Tada's
office at 9 o'clock.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, WEDNESDAY, DECEMBER 4, 1935    126llc

Ho Reaches Peiping;
Trip Taken Following
Doihara Phone Talks

Conferences On North
China Affairs To Con-
tinue In Old Capital

CHINESE FEEL
SITUATION BETTER

Doihara Working Hard
To Gain Big Area
Without Fight

PEIPING, Dec. 3.—(Reuters).—
General Ho Ying-chin, the Chinese
War Minister, who has been sent
to North China by the Nanking
Government to devise some solution
of the problem arising from the
so-called autonomy movement, arriv-
ed here at 6.35 o'clock this evening.
His arrival followed three drama-
tic telephone conversations that he
had during the night with Major-
General Kenji Doihara, his princi-
pal protagonist in the North China
drama.
General Ho was in Paotingfu, the
seat of the Hopei Provincial Govern-
ment, where he had been conferr-
ing with General Shang Chen, Gov-
ernor of Hopei, and other North
China leaders, and Major-General
Doihara was in Peiping.
"Moderately satisfactory" is the
description given in reliable Chinese
quarters to the conversations, the
first of which took place at 11
o'clock as the result of a call put in
by General Ho. Later, Major-Gen-
eral Doihara called up the War
Minister, and, finally, at 3 o'clock
this morning, General Ho telephon-
ed a second time to the Japanese
officer.
The Minister of War left his
special train at the Paotingfu sta-
tion at 10.30 this morning, arriving
within half an hour at the Hopei
Government offices, where talks took
place with General Shang Chen, offi-
cials and others. At 11.30 General
Ho, accompanied by Mr. Wang
Peng-yang, Secretary of the War
Ministry, and other officials, left
Paotingfu by special train for Peip-
ing, arriving here at 6.35 this even-
ing. He was met at the station by
General Sung Cheh-yuan, Garrison
Commander of Peiping and Tientsin,
and other officials.
General Ho and a number of offi-
cials left by special train for Pao-
tingfu this morning, returning by
another special train this evening.
It is understood that the War Minis-
ter will remain in Peiping for sev-
eral days.
Reports that General Ho had re-
ceived instructions from Nanking to
accept the Japanese demands for au-
tonomy in North China were denied
in responsible quarters. It was stat-
ed that the War Minister's mission
was to seek a solution of the prob-
lem which would be acceptable to
both the Central Government and
the people of North China.

Paotingfu Bustling
With a steady stream of officials
arriving from Peiping, Paotingfu
hummed with activity throughout
the day. Nothing was divulged,
however, concerning the progress of
General Ho's negotiations, although
he was reported to have been again
in telephonic communication with
Peiping.
General Chin Teh-chun, Mayor of
Peiping, today denied the report
that General Sung Cheh-yuan, Gar-
rison Commander of Peiping and
Tientsin, went yesterday to Pao-
tingfu, to which center he was re-
ported to have traveled secretly
to meet General Ho.
General Sung was, however, re-
presented at the provincial seat by
two officials, General Meng Chi-
chung and Mr. Lei Shou-ying. Mr.
Lei, who arrived there this morning,
carried a long report from General
Sung for presentation to General Ho.
Several Japanese, including one
alleged to be an adviser to Mr. Yin
Ju-keng leader of the so-called
autonomous government of East
Hopei, also arrived at Paotingfu
this morning, but up to early this
evening none of them had gained
access to the Chinese War Minis-
ter.
Some alarm was felt by the in-
habitants of Paotingfu this morn-
ing when several Japanese air-
planes made their appearance and
circled over the city. They remain-
ed aloft for several hours.
General Hsiung Shih-hui, chair-
man of the Hopei provincial gov-
ernment, who accompanied General
Ho when he left Nanking for North
China, reached Peiping this morn-
ing.
He follows General Chen Yi,
Governor of Fukien, who also left
Nanking with General Ho, and
who arrived here yesterday from
Tientsin, where he interviewed Lt.-
Gen. [Tashiro], commander of the Jap-
anese troops in North China.

Doihara Working Hard
Well-informed foreign sources de-
clare that Major-General Doihara
is indicated clearly the importance
placed on the outcome of the
task to which he had set his hand
—that of winning for Japan, ac-
tually or practically, a vast slice
of territory without military opera-
tions.
Unquestionably, he is fighting the
hardest diplomatic battle of his
uniformly successful career.
Ten prominent educators, includ-
ing representatives of five universi-
ties, the Academia Sinica, and the
National Library, have despatched
a telegram to the Executive Yuan
at Nanking concerning public feel-
ing in North China.
The message read:
"In the past two days there have
appeared in the press several tele-
grams giving the impression that
there is a public sentiment in North
China for local autonomy.
"From personal observation we
now positively that, despite the
handbills distributed by persons
hired for the purpose, no section of
the population of any profession or
trade has any desire for autonomy
or separation from the Central
Government.
"We hope you will not be misled
by these telegrams. We hope that
both the Central and local authori-
ties will use all the means at their
disposal to maintain territorial and
administrative integrity."

Peiping Impression That
Events In North Are Now
Heading Towards Crisis

PEIPING MILITARY COUNCIL WINDS UP
ITS AFFAIRS IN ACCORDANCE WITH
INSTRUCTIONS FROM NANKING

SECRET CONFERENCE OF CHINESE
LEADERS LASTS TILL 4 A.M.

Important Telegram Sent To Nanking Asking For
More Specific Instructions; Tokyo Does Not
Intend To Reply To Protest On Seizure

PEIPING, Nov. 30.—The Peiping Military Council wound up its affairs to-day in accordance with instructions from Nanking.

Hereafter, matters previously handled by the Council will be dealt with by the Nanking Military Council.

Meanwhile, there is a general impression that events here are rapidly heading for a crisis, which may come as soon as Monday.

It is learned that a secret conference of local Chinese leaders lasted from last evening till four o'clock this morning, at the conclusion of which an important telegram was dispatched to Nanking asking for more specific instructions.

It is understood that the telegram was addressed to General Chiang Kai-shek, Dr. H. H. Kung, Finance Minister, and General Ho Ying-chin, Minister of war.

According to the Japanese military spokesman, the telegram is to the effect that the autonomy movement developing now is beyond the powers of the local authorities to stop.

Hopei And Chahar Only?

On the other hand, well-informed Chinese sources declare that the Japanese have expressed the view that the autonomy of Hopei and Chahar would satisfy them and that the area might still be nominally under Nanking.

It is reported that Major-General Doihara, who, it was rumoured, had intended to leave to-day, is now remaining for another two or three days.

Chinese Conferences

The chief of staff of General Sung Cheh-yuan, garrison commander of Peiping and Tientsin, who visited Paotingfu on Wednesday to see General Shang Chen, chairman of Hopei, and to invite him to come to Peiping, returned this afternoon, not with General Shang Chen but with his chief of staff.

The latter held a conference with General Sung this evening, but the result is not known.

Loyalty Pledged

Telegrams pledging their loyalty to the Government were sent to Nanking to-day by the Labour Union of Peiping and the Farmers' Union of Hopei Province.

"We swear to remain loyal to our Central Government and to resist any action taken by the puppet regime of the self-styled East Hopei Autonomous Government to consolidate its position," declared the former, while the telegram of the Farmers' Union read, in part:

"We solemnly declare that we denounce the so-called East Hopei Autonomous Government.

"We are determined to have no dealings with the puppet regime, and we are ready to give every support to our Government in the maintenance of territorial integrity in China."—Reuters.

Japan Not To Reply

TOKYO, Nov. 30.—The Japanese Government will not reply to the Chinese protest on the alleged seizure of Fengtai junction by Japanese troops on Thursday, on the ground that such action would be "unnecessary, as the question was already been settled."

This was the statement made today by a spokesman of the Foreign Office, who said that a report on the subject had been received this morning from Mr. A. Ariyoshi, Japanese Ambassador to China.

The other representation protested against the occupation of the Fengtai and Changyimen railway stations in the vicinity of Peiping, on the ground that it constituted a violation of China’s sovereignty. The two Notes were handed by the Waichiachpu to Mr. Yakichiro Suma, Japanese Consul-General here. The Chinese Government stressed its desire to settle the Northern problems through diplomatic channels, and asserted that the autonomy movement did not represent “popular desires.” The second Note asked for the immediate and complete evacuation of the two stations, and for a guarantee against the recurrence of similar incidents.

CHINA IS NOT PREPARING FOR IT

General Sung Cheh-yuan Declines To Take Up
Pacification Post For Chahar And Hopei;
Tokyo Says Movement Is Internal Affair

PEIPING, Nov. 28.—The Japanese military spokesman here, questioned to-day concerning the situation at Fengtai and Changyimen, the two railway stations occupied yesterday by Japanese troops, said that the main forces there were withdrawn this morning, but a few men had been left behind to check the movement of rolling stock.

The spokesman said that, despite Chinese denials that rolling stock was being withdrawn from North China, the Japanese believed that such evacuation was proceeding. They also believed that one third of the rolling stock of the Peiping-Hankow Railway was now concentrated south of the Yellow River.

The Japanese, he continued, knew that there were 1,300 cars on the northern section of the line on November 15, but, 10 days later, this number had been reduced to 900.

Asked the reason why the Japanese were so concerned over the alleged removal of rolling stock to the south, the spokesman said that the withdrawal looked like preparation for war.

“We don’t wish for war,” he declared, “and we hope China doesn’t prepare for war.”

The spokesman denied that the Japanese themselves had actually prevented any rolling stock being moved, saying that the local authorities did not wish any stock to be evacuated and so had stopped the evacuation.

Surprise In Peiping

The withdrawal of the Japanese troops from Fengtai and Changyimen came as a surprise to Peiping in view of the statement by the Japanese military spokesman yesterday that the two stations had been occupied “to protect communications and prevent the removal southward of Peiping of rolling stock.”

Fengtai is an important junction 12 miles south of Peiping, while Changyimen is situated about 300 yards outside the south-west gate of the city.—Reuter.

PEIPING, Nov. 28.—General Sung Cheh-yuan, garrison commander of Peiping and Tientsin, who has just declined the new appointment of Pacification Commissioner for Hopei and Chahar, is being subjected to terrific Japanese pressure, according to reliable Chinese sources.

Well-informed observers, foreign as well as Chinese, believe that the present situation cannot long be maintained, and they voice the opinion that before many days the status of Hopei and Chahar is likely to undergo a change.

It is widely reported to-day that an invitation from General Sung to General Han Fu-chu, chairman of the Shantung Provincial Government, and General Shang Chen, chairman of Hopei, to come to Peiping to discuss the situation has been turned down.

Meanwhile, there is a feeling among those close to General Sung that he has declined his new post because the appointment has come too late.

These circles point out that if the appointment had been made two months ago, the present situation in North China could have been avoided.

It is also stated that General Sung desires rather more authority than the latest appointment would give him, meaning that he probably thinks the appointment should also carry the provincial chairmanship of Hopei, which would enable him to replace the troops of General Shang Chen in Tientsin with his own.—Reuter.

“Since it is already difficult to safeguard the security of Peiping and Tientsin,” he added, “I fear that I cannot undertake the heavier responsibility of pacifying Hopei and Chahar.”

"There are reports," he added, "that I have fled. This is absolutely untrue. I will remain here, and I defy the Nanking authorities to arrest me."

Japanese comment on General Ho's appointment is not yet available, but it is safe to say that, when the Minister of War was in Peiping before, he enjoyed the confidence of the Japanese. It remains to be seen whether, with the idea of autonomy now fixedly in front of them, they will receive him as direct representative of the Executive Yuan on the same footing.

General Shang Chen, chairman of Hopei, formerly dismissed Mr. Yin to-day as Administrative Inspector of the demilitarized zone.

A body of educators from Peiping universities called on General Sung last night and spoke strongly against autonomy. In reply General Sung said he would abide by the instructions of the National Government.

General Hsu Yung-chang, chairman of Shansi, called on General Sung this morning and conferred with him on the North China situation. The result was not divulged.

Mysterious Request

It is reliably stated that the Japanese military authorities have requested the railway authorities to concentrate six trains—three at Tientsin and three at Fengtai—for the use of the Japanese.

This request has already been complied with, but the reason for it remains a mystery.

General Yen Hsi-shan, Pacification Commissioner for Shansi, arrived at Taiyuanfu from Nanking yesterday afternoon in General Chiang Kai-shek's aeroplane.

It will be recalled that, when Major-Doihara was here last week, the Japanese military spokesman stated that he (Major-General Doihara) would probably visit General Yen Hsi-shan on his return from Nanking. Observers are watching with great interest whether the "Lawrence of Manchuria" will now go to Shansi.

Japanese troops who arrived here yesterday afternoon were quartered outside the Legation quarters.—Reuter.

Officials Refuse To Serve Yin;
Bogus "Foreign Minister" Quits

Dissensions seem to be rife in the
so-called "East Hopei Autonomous
Council for Defense against Com-
munism," as Mr. Hou Shih, who
was reported to have been appoint-

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Wednesday, November 27, 1935

Indignation Over
'Traitor' In North

Various Bodies Demand
Punitive Expedition
Against Yin

Vigorously denouncing Yin Ju-keng, chairman of te "East Hopei Autonomous Government," as a traitor, the Shanghai Chamber of Commerce, the General Labor Union the Shanghai Civic Association and the Federation of Secondary Schools have telegraphed the Central Government and North China authorities demanding the immediate launching of a punitive expedition against the rebel.

The telegrams also urged the Central Government and high administrative officials in North China to exert their efforts to maintain the territorial sovereignty of the country. Some of the appeals were addressed directly to General Sun Chen-yuan, the newly appointed Pacification Commander for Chahar and Hopei Provinces, whose name has been linked to a plot to create an "Autonomous Government of North China of the Republic of China."

Southwest Condemns

The Southwest Political Council and Southwest Executive Department of the Kuomintang in Canton are also to join the nation-wide condemnation of the separation movement launched by Yin in Tungchow on Monday. Circular telegrams are being drafted by the Southwest leaders to condemn Yin and to suggest to the Nanking authorities concrete steps to be taken to prevent spreading of the movement.

According to the Shun Pao, Mr. Hsiao Fu-chen, one of the most influential political leaders in Canton, declared in an interview that he advocates the launching of an punitive drive against the "traitor."

Yin Stigmatized As Outcast

Yin, those wife is a Japanese and whose sister is the daughter-in-law of Cheng Shao-su, former premier of Manchukuo, has been officially condemned as an "outcast of mankind." In a mandate issued by the National Government, Yin was condemned as "heartless and mad, casting himself out from the mankind."

The mandate orders arrest of the rebel leader and his severe punishment. The Hopei Provincial Government was told to relieve Yin of his office as Administrative commissioner of the Demilitarized Zone.

Japanese Seize Railway Station Outside Peiping; Act
Declared Part Of Maneuvers; “All Will Be Handed Back
Afterwards;” Troop Train Passes Shanhaikuan South

Train Officials Persuade
Warriors To Permit
Operation Of Schedule

Force Of 90 Nipponese Soldiers Take
Railway Depot At Fengtai
At 5 A.M. Today

Passenger Coaches, Freight Cars, Chinese Army
Telephone Lines Commandeered; Act
Arouses More Anxiety

“EXERCISES” NEAR “AUTONOMOUS” REGION

Movements Coincide With Tension

(Reuter's Agency)
PEIPING, Nov. 27.—Ninety Japanese soldiers, who left here
at 5 o'clock this morning have taken over control of the Fengtai
railway station according to reports from reliable Chinese sources.
The reports state that, when the Japanese soldiers arrived at
the Fengtai station, they attempted to hold up traffic but were
persuaded by the railway officials to allow trains to proceed
normally.
The troops are stated to have commandeered a number of
passenger coaches and freight wagons belonging to the Peking-
Hankow railway, and also to have
taken over the Chinese military
telephone lines.
The Fengtai station is a large
junction 12 miles south of Peiping,
on the line to Tientsin, and near
the boundary of the so-called "East
Hopei Autonomous State" proclaimed
in the Demilitarized Zone on
Monday by Mr. Yin Ju-keng.
Some observers attribute the
move to reports of contemplated
action by Chinese troops against
the new regime—which the Japanese claim would be an infringement of the Tangku Truce (by
which the Demilitarized Zone was
established in May, 1933).

A semi-official Japanese explanation of the affair is that troops
from Tangshan and the Peiping
Embassy Guard are holding exercises which call for an attack on
the Fengtai station. Its occupation,
and the seizure of rolling-stock and
telephone lines, as they would do
during a real war. When the
exercises are completed, it is stated
"all will be handed back."
The seizure of the Fengtai station, railway coaches and telephone
lines is causing considerable nervousness among the Chinese,
although it follows Japanese

customs of some years past here of
holding maneuvers in Chinese territory during times of political
tension.

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Wednesday, November 27, 1935

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, WEDNESDAY, NOVEMBER 27, 1935
Arrest Of Yin Ju-keng
Ordered By Nanking But
Revolt Official Laughs

Executive Yuan Decides Upon Sweeping Changes
In North China, Involving The Dispatch Of
General Ho Ying-chin To Peiping

GENERAL SHANG CHEN ISSUES ORDERS TO
OFFICIALS NOT TO BE DECEIVED

NANKING, Nov. 26. The Central authorities acted to-day to reassert their authority in North China when the Executive Yuan, after a meeting this morning, ordered the Hopei Provincial Government to arrest Mr. Yin Ju-keng self-proclaimed head of the new "East Hopei Autonomous Government," which was inaugurated at Tungchow, in the Demilitarized Zone, yesterday.

Several sweeping changes in the administration of North China were also ordered, including: Abolition of the Peiping Branch Military Council and the transfer of its functions to the Military Affairs Commission, of which General Chiang Kai-shek is chairman; appointment of General Ho Ying-chin, the War Minister, to be resident representative of the Executive Yuan at Peiping; appointment of General Sung Cheh-yuan, garrison commander of Peiping and Tientsin, to fill the new office of Pacification Commissioner of Hopei and Chahar.

Much interest was aroused in Nanking this afternoon when it became known that General Yen Hsi-shan, Pacification Commissioner for Shansi, had left suddenly in General Chiang Kai-shek's aeroplane for Taiyuan, Shansi.

General Yen came to Nanking on October 26 with the reported object of obtaining certain assurances from the Central authorities regarding autonomist pressure in North China, and he was not expected to leave again so soon.

On his arrival at Taiyuan it is stated that he will proceed to Hopien, his native village, to make preparations to commemorate the anniversary of his father's death.

Circumstances suggest that the assurances he sought have not been lacking.—Reuter.

Yin Laughs

TUNGCHOW, Nov. 26.—Mr. Yin Ju-keng, Chairman of the "East Hopei Autonomous Government," which came into being yesterday, laughed to-night at the report that the Nanking Government had ordered his arrest.

Interviewed at the offices of the new administration here, Mr. Yin said he has "too busy to bother about that."

"I have other more important questions to think about," he remarked.

To-morrow, the new Government plans to open an office at Tongshan to control the revenue from the Peiping-Liaoning Railway on a 160-mile stretch from Hsinho to Shanhaikwan.—Rengo.

Planes Over Tientsin

TIENTSIN, Nov. 26.—After its disturbing experience yesterday, when autonomist elements made an abortive attempt to stage a coup, the Chinese city here was quiet to-day.

Some excitement was caused this morning when two Japanese aeroplanes were seen flying over the city. The machines circled over Tientsin almost the whole day long, and finally alighted in a field in the vicinity of the Nankai Race Course, which the Japanese are at present using as an aerodrome.

Under the supervision of Japanese officers, Chinese coolies were busy to-day levelling a plot of land adjoining the International Race Course and the railway. It is reported that the field will be used for aviation purposes.

The report that martial law has been proclaimed in the Japanese Concession here is without foundation.

Two hundred Japanese troops left Lanchien this morning for Peiping.—Reuter.

Watching Mr. Yin

PEIPING, Nov. 26. The attitude of the Central Government towards the movement of Mr. Yin Ju-keng, self-proclaimed head of the new "East Hopei Autonomous Government," was made known to the Chinese authorities in North China to-day.

General Sung Cheh-yuan, Garrison Commander of Peiping and Tientsin, is understood to have received instructions from the capital stating that Nanking cannot, under any circumstances, recognize the movement.

At the same time, the authorities here are advised to watch Mr. Yin's movements, but to avoid any action which might give rise to diplomatic complications over the Demilitarised Zone.

A number of Chinese magistrates from the Zone arrived in Paoting to-day to protest to General Shang Chen, Chairman of Hopei, against Mr. Yin's action.

Japanese Troop Moves

Meanwhile, the Japanese military strength here has been increased. A detachment of 225 men arrived by train at 4 o'clock this afternoon from Luantung, and it is believed that another 275 are on their way.

According to the official reason given, the despatch of the new troops to Peiping is to allow them to participate in manoeuvres with the Japanese Embassy Guard.

Reliable Chinese reports states that several thousand Japanese troops have penetrated Kupeikow and are now stationed between Kupeikow and Miyun.

The number is probably exaggerated, but it seems definite that a considerable number have penetrated the Wall, but the reason is not apparent.

A common situation prevails in connection with the establishment of the so-called "Autonomous Government of East Hopei" by Mr. Yin Ju-keng.

Mr. Yin has appointed members of his new Council of Nine to supervise the railways running through the "autonomous area" as well as the collection of taxes.

He is establishing an office in Tangshan with the object of taking over the railway from Hsinho to Shanhaikwan, a stretch of about 160 miles.

Trains controlled by the ordinary railway authorities are, however, still running normally from Peiping to Tungchow and Shanhaikwan, and Mr. Yin's next move is being awaited with interest.

Peiping is quiet, and there is no sign yet of the so-called autonomous movement spreading.

Doihara Inactive

Major-General Doihara, of the Kwantung Army, who arrived here yesterday from Tientsin, remains apparently inactive, and there is a feeling that he will await the outcome of the expected meeting between General Chiang Kai-shek and Mr. Ariyoshi, the Japanese Ambassador to China, before advancing any more "suggestions."

A Japanese military spokesman stated that General Daihara still had no official mission in Peiping.

It is generally believed that Mr. Yin's declaration is partly a gesture intended to counteract the failure of autonomist elements to secure the alienation of the five northern provinces, as well as a threat to Nanking to accelerate the conversations with Japan.

It is interesting to note that General Sung Cheh-yuen, Garrison Commander of Peiping and Tientsin, General Chin Teh-chun, Mayor of Peiping, and General Hsiao Cheng-yin, Governor of Chahar, had to travel through the "autonomous" area when they returned to Peiping from Tientsin yesterday.

Besides the Demilitarized Zone, Mr. Yin claims control over the neighbouring district of Changping, north of Peiping, and the three districts of Hsiangho, Paoti and Ningho, between Peiping and Tientsin.—Reuter.

GENERAL SHANG CHEN

Relief In Nanking
NANKING, Nov. 26. There was a distinct feeling of relief in Chinese circles here this morning when they learnt that the eventful day experienced by Tientsin yesterday had passed without any further untoward incident.
Chinese quarters, however, are completely puzzled by the attempt of "autonomist" coup there yesterday, which started with such ominous possibilities, but yet ended in such a tame manner.
The question "What next?" is being asked everywhere, and official circles hesitate to pass any judgment on the situation, preferring to wait and watch further developments.—Reuter.

Gen. Shang Chen's Attitude
PAOTINGFU, Nov. 26. Immediate suppression of the autonomy movement, by armed force if necessary, was urged this morning by General Shang Chen, Chairman of the Hopei Provincial Government, in a telegram to General Sung Cheh-yuan, Commander of the Tientsin-Peiping Garrison.
Simultaneously, General Shang sent a circular despatch to all the hsien magistrates in the Province and chiefs of Peace Preservation Corps units urging them to refuse to obey orders issued by the "self-styled autonomous Government" and counselling a "prudent attitude." Rengo.

$10,000,000 Income
PEIPING, Nov. 26. The newly-formed autonomous Government, comprising 25 hsien, will have at its disposal an annual income of $10,000,000, the Kokutsu News Agency said to-day.
The revenues will include local taxes, totalling $2,800,000; Provincial levies, amounting to $2,000,-000, and $5,000,000 in duties formerly collected by the Central Government.
A specially appointed committee of seven will be in charge of the gathering and disbursement of these sums.
The new Government will, however, take special precautions to avoid friction with Foreign Powers in connection with the collection of the Customs taxes and the Salt Gabelle, the news agency said. —Rengo.

Primarily Economic.
DAIREN, Nov. 26.—Herr Hans Troebst, the Manchurian correspondent of the Deutsche Nachrichten Bureau, returned here to-day from Tientsin, whither he went to interview Major-General Tada, Commander of the Japanese Garrison in North China.
The North China autonomy movement, General Tada is reported to have told Herr Troebst, is primarily economic. "It might be calm one day, and flash out in thunders and lightning another day, but we are ready to deal with any emergency here."
The General is stated to have added that nobody could foretell how the crisis would end.—Reuter.

Leith-Ross's Activities
TOKYO, Nov. 26.—Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, British economic expert, to-day was charged by Japanese officials with having run counter to his assertions here and in Shanghai that his visit to China was for the purpose of investigation and that he had no political objective.
This criticism was based on an official report received by the Foreign Office to-day from Mr. Shigeru Kawagoe, Japanese Consul-General in Tientsin, quoting statements attributed to Sir Frederick by the "Tientsin and Peking Times," a British publication.

According to this despatch the British expert told correspondents, in an interview given at the British Consulate-General on Saturday, that he was convinced that the economic separation of North China could not last.
He is further quoted as having declared that no American or European Power, and particularly Britain, would give assistance to any autonomous Government in North China.
This, Japanese officials hold, constitutes interference in North China politics.
Sir Frederick's reported assertion that while he did not know how the people felt about it he believed that the bankers of North China had full confidence in the Central Bank of China and that they welcomed the monetary reforms was also held objectionable. —Rengo.

"Disguised" Soldiers
TIENTSIN, Nov. 26. Japanese forces were on guard here to-day following reports that Chinese regulars were entering the city in large numbers disguised as policemen from the Bureau of Public Safety.
Should the report be confirmed, the Japanese military authorities will demand complete withdrawal of these allegedly "smuggled" effectives on the ground that the presence of Chinese troops in Tientsin constitutes a breach of the Boxer Protocol, a spokesman at headquarters said.
According to rumours being widely circulated, General Shang Chen, Chairman of the Hopei Provincial Government and concurrently commander of the Tientsin-Tangku Garrison, ordered the 112th and 114th Divisions of the Thirty-Second Army, under his command, to concentrate at Yangliucheng and Chunliangcheng near Tientsin.
Part of these forces is said to have reached Tsaochayen, Tunghsiang and Hsiaoyingmen, allegedly disguised in police uniforms. Two battalions are already rumoured to have entered the city. —Rengo.

Ho Not Yet Decided
NANKING, Nov. 26.—Circles in close touch with General Ho Ying-chin, Minister of War, stated to-day that he had not yet decided when to proceed to Peiping to assume his new post of resident representative of the Executive Yuan at Peiping.—Reuter.

Consolidated Tax Bureau
NANKING, Nov. 26.—The Ministry of Finance received a telegram to-day from the Consolidated Tax Bureau in Tangshan saying that Mr. Yin Ju-keng had demanded the surrender of the Bureau.
In reply, the Ministry instructed the head of the Bureau to resist the demand and to carry on his functions as usual.
Meanwhile, the Control Yuan has sent a petition to the National Government, asking that the Hopei authorities be instructed to take drastic effective measures against Mr. Yin.—Reuter.

Sino-Japanese Relations
NANKING, Nov. 26. The Chinese Charge d'Affaires in Tokyo telegraphed to the Foreign Office to-day reporting on his conversation with Mr. Shigemitsu yesterday.
The telegram it is understood stated that the Japanese Foreign Office favoured further exchanges of opinion with a view to improving the relations between China and Japan.
Mr Y. Suma, the Japanese Consul in Nanking, and Colonel Son Anemiya, military attache, interviewed Mr. Tang Yu-jen, Vice Foreign Minister, this afternoon. Reuter.

Japanese Army Impartial
TIENTSIN Nov. 26. Chinese authorities were to-day backed by the Japanese Army in their efforts to curb disturbances by "opportunists, who, actuated by personal motives, seek to utilize the popular desire for autonomy to further their own ends."
The use of force in suppressing "the people's natural inclinations, however," will "not help in solving the present situation," a spokesman for the headquarters of the Japanese forces in North China said to-night.
"We are of the opinion that it is not wise for the Chinese authorities merely to seek to suppress the wishes of the people of North China," he added. "We believe that the officials should make a careful investigation of the situation so as to acquire a correct insight into the people's natural inclinations and act accordingly so as to lead them into the proper channels. A mere high-handed policy will not help in solving the present situation."
The spokesman, after criticizing the alleged "bitter stubbornness of the Nanking authorities in refusing to see the truth," said the Japanese Army would "always remain impartial."—Rengo.

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Tuesday, November 26, 1935

N. China Feeling
Tense, Uncertain;
Part 'Autonomy'

Tiny Area Is Declared
Independent; A Sop
To Doihara?

MARTIAL LAW FOR
TIENTSIN, PEIPING

Chinese Press Allowed
To Print Story Of
Tungchow Event

The North China situation was both tense and uncertain today, according to reports reaching Shanghai through various sources.

Autonomy in the zone demilitarized by the Tangku Truce was an accomplished fact, but whether any effort would be made to extend the "autonomy" movement farther was not clear.

Since the demilitarized zone has always been, in effect, under Japanese rule, the formal "inauguration" of an "autonomous government" there was not, in itself, regarded by local observers as either important or significant except that no revenue from the area will now go to Nanking. It was suggested by one Western diplomatic official that the step had been taken primarily to save General Dohara's face in view of the recent apparent repudiation by Tokyo of his report efforts to achieve "autonomy" in all of North China.

Dolhara In Peiping

However, General Dolhara has again returned to Peiping—which he left after the first effort at "autonomy" had failed—and, according to Chinese reports, 20 railway coaches of Japanese troops are also en route from "Manchukuo" to the old capital.

Martial law, which was declared yesterday in Tientsin, was also declared in Peiping at midnight last night, but at the present it is scheduled to prevail only at night.

Further evidence that Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, British economic advisor is probably doing more than merely observing developments is suggested in a dispatch from Tokyo which quotes a Foreign Office spokesman as severely criticizing him for his activities in China. Sir Frederick went to North China immediately after the first effort toward "autonomy" there.

The Tungchow "Inauguration"

Great prominence is given in all the Chinese newspapers this morning to reports of the "inauguration" yesterday at Tungchow of the new "Autonomous Government of East Hopei" under the direction of Mr. Yin Ju-keng, Administrative Commissioner of the Demilitarized Zone.

The amount of space devoted to the reports, which are given in detail in all the papers, indicate that the press dispatches were permitted to flow freely from the North without interference by local censors.

330 Square Miles

An army of 50 Chinese and foreign press correspondents from Peiping and Tientsin went to Tungchow, "capital" of the new "regime," to "cover" the "inauguration" of the "Government" under Yin. A representative of the Sin Wen Pao states that only 24 districts are included in the administration, and these comprise a little over 1600 square li (about 330 square miles). Within this territory there are about 4,600,000 people, mostly farmers and villagers.

The total local revenue of all the 24 districts each year is around $2,600,000; national revenue amounts to $5,000,000, exclusive of Customs, railway and salt taxes. Several hundred thousand dollars worth of silver dollars and subsidiary coins is in circulation in these districts.

Small Fighting Force

The fighting force of this area is comparatively small and insignificant, comprising, it is estimated at present, 15,000 members of the Peace Preservation Corps and about 20,000 militiamen.

The Chinese papers state that Yin has named his "administration" the "Anti-Red Defense Self-Government Council." The districts under this "rule" include Ningho, Hsiangho, Paoti, Changping, Lanyu, Funing, Changli, Chieuan, Luhng, Lohsien, Lotung, Fengjun, Tsunhua, Hsinglung, Yutun, Pingku, Miyun, Huajao, Sanho, Suhsien, Shunyi and Tungshien.

Nanking On The Watch

A dispatch from Nanking states that the Central Government is watching developments in the North with the closest interest. According to a spokesman of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Government has adopted effective measures to cope with the situation.

A message from Peiping states that Yin has six or seven Japanese "advisers" in Tungchow. His Japanese wife is still in Peiping. Yin has also opened a "Peiping office" by which he will maintain contacts with the officials there.

According to the China Times, Yin Ju-keng is a native of Chekiang and is 47 years of age. He was educated in Japan, and is well-known as having pro-Japanese sympathies.

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, NOVEMBER 25, 1935

Autonomy in
North China
Commencing

Independence as Defence
Against Communism

EDUCATORS EXPRESS
OPPOSITION

Peiping, Nov. 24
Twenty-five hsien of Eastern Hopei will form an autonomous federation for joint defence against communism, under the terms of a proclamation made today by Mr. Yin Ju-keng, Administrative Commissioner of the Luantung Demilitarized Zone.

The new administration will be named "The East Hopei Autonomous Council for Defence Against Communism" and will have its headquarters in Tangchow.

Formal establishment of the Council is scheduled to take place tomorrow.

According to the proclamation the Council will recognize the sovereignty of the Republic of China, and will observe existing laws with the addition of any regulations deemed necessary because of local conditions. All national revenues, will be administered by the Council, the document stated.

The edict severely upbraided alleged Kuomintang maladministration.

The twenty-five hsien will include. Mr. Yin's proclamation further stated, seven districts in addition to the 18 of the demilitarized zone. These are Ningho, Paoting, Hsiangho, Changping, Yenching, Lunmen and Chuncheng.--Rengo.

Uneasiness in Tientsin

Tientsin, Nov. 24.
The collapse of the autonomy negotiations is expected to lead to a renewal of attempts to seize administrative power in Tientsin.

The situation here last night was tense owing to rumours of an impending effort by gunmen, wearing police uniforms, to occupy important parts of the city. The police, however, turned out last night in their summer uniforms in an effort to checkmate the plotters, several of whom were arrested.

"Self-government" demonstrators today distributed handbills from motor cars which were decorated with the emblem of the Blue Swastika Society. The handbills, which urged the overthrow of the Nanking Government and opposition to Nanking's monetary policy, were also pasted on walls, but these were obliterated by spectators after they had been pasted up.

It is reported that should the efforts of the autonomists fail in Tientsin, the Peace Preservation Corps in the Demilitarized Zone will be utilized as the spearhead for the movement, following which the existing military heads will be overthrown--Reuter.

Scholars Oppose Move

Peiping, Nov. 24.
Strong opposition to any movement aiming at the detachment of North China from the Nanking Government is expressed in a circular telegram issued to-day by the chancellors and deans of four government universities, including the Tsing Hua and National Universities in Peiping.

The telegram, which, among others, is signed by Dr. Chiang Mon-lin, Chancellor of the National University, Peiping, and Dr. Hu Shih, the famous philosopher and educator, also urges the National Government to do everything possible to maintain the territorial and administrative integrity of China.

The telegram was issued after a joint meeting at which the following resolution was unanimously adopted:
"Since there have appeared statements in the press purporting to represent the people in this region as favouring the so-called autonomy movement, we, members of universities and other cultural institutions in Peiping, do solemnly declare that we are utterly opposed to any movement tending to detach any region of China from the jurisdiction of the Central Government, or to upset the special political organ for such region.
"We urge the Central Government to use the energies of the entire nation to maintain the territorial and administrative integrity of the country."

Signatories to the telegram also include the Chancellor of Yenching University.--Reuter.

THE CHINA PRESS, TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 26, 1935

Tientsin Quiet As
Coup Fizzles Out;
Mob Harries "Rebels"

Insurgents Establish
Headquarters But
Finally Disperse

JAPANESE, POLICE
SECURE EVACUATION

Crowd Attacks Building
Of Insurrectos, Causes
Temporary Panic

TIENTSIN, Nov. 25.—(Reuter).—
All was quiet in Tientsin tonight
after an anxious day during which
an attempted coup by autonomist
elements, at one stage threatening
serious trouble, completely fizzled
out.

Early this morning several hundred rebel-demonstrators, some in
plain-clothes, some wearing uniform, and many carrying arms, assembled in front of the Municipal
offices and the headquarters of the
Peace Preservation Corps, waving
banners and shouting slogans.

Persuaded to depart, the main
body, their ranks continually swelled by new arrivals, who drove up
in trucks, marched to the Tungmaliu, Tientsin's main street, and
seized a public lecture hall.

Posting guards round the building, they announced a mass meeting for the purpose of "declaring
self-government" and demanding
the abdication of the Chinese
authorities.

They proclaimed themselves to be
alternatively members of the "North
China People's Self-Defense Corps"
and the "North China Farmers'
Self-Salvation Corps," while the
armed guards who were to protect
the new "regime" were described as
"Dare-to-Die" men.

Chinese police and units of the
Peace Preservation Corps were
called out in strength and mounted
guard with fixed bayonets at various
centers throughout the Chinese-controlled city. They were instructed to maintain order, but not to
fire.

Asked To Capitulate

Later, representatives of the
police and the Japanese military
authorities approached the rebels'
headquarters and urged them to
evacuate. Many of them did so, but
200 "die-hards" remained despite all
persuasion, announcing that they
would not tolerate extreme action
by the police.

Meanwhile, the police were confronted by groups of demonstrators
at various points in the city.

Uniformed rebels visited the railway offices and posted a guard outside, but later were prevailed upon
to depart. Others were busy distributing pamphlets and sticking up
notices demanding "self-government."

Crowds gathered to watch the
proceedings, milling in their thousands in the vicinity of Tungmaliu.
At first they were good-humored,
although evidently out of sympathy
with the demonstrators, and watched events with cynical amusement.
In the afternoon, however, bored
with inactivity, some of the rowdier elements bore down on the
rebels' headquarters, tore up their
banners and inscriptions, and caused panic among the guards, who
took refuge inside the building,
jeers accompanying their retreat.

Elsewhere the police quickly regained control of affairs, but they
had the greatest difficulty in checking the crowds along Tungmaliu,
where traffic was completely disrupted for some time.

Eventually, however, the remnants
of the rebels in the lecture hall
were persuaded to disperse, many
of them discarding their uniforms,
and gradually the onlookers followed their example.

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 26, 1935

Plans Well Advanced
Tientsin, Nov. 24
Plans for the establishment of an autonomous government to rule Eastern Hopei province were far advanced here to-day. The leaders of the movement are Chinese who are considered to be sympathetic with Japanese policies in North China.
A declaration in the name of Mr. Yin Ju-keng, Special Administrative Inspector for the Luanchow-Shanhaikwan Area of the Demilitarized Zone stated that the new regime is to be inaugurated formally at 9 a.m. on Monday. According to Mr. Yin's declaration the governing body is to be called the Autonomous Council for the Prevention of Communism in Eastern Hopei, and the seat of government is to be established at Tungchow, between Peiping and the border of the Demilitarized Zone.
The highest personnel of the proposed new government was decided on Saturday night at a secret meeting in the home of General Shih Yu-san, according to reliable information obtained here to-day. General Shih himself is to be Chairman of the Military Commission. Mr. Pai Chien-wu, who led the abortive assault on Peiping from Fengtai Station last June, was chosen garrison commander. Since his Fengtai adventure, Pai is understood to have been hiding in the Demilitarized Zone, where he was reported to be associated with a group of insurgents.
The following were named members of the Military Commission: Messrs. Chang Ching-yi, Chang Yin-tien, Li Hai-tien, Li Teh-lu, Chao Lei, and Wang Tao-yi.
Mr. Chi Si-yuan was appointed Chairman of the Political Commission, which includes the following among its members:—Messrs. Liu Ta-lung, Hao Peng, Chien Chun-kai, Wu Yi-ting, Wang Chien-chung, Mao Hs ang-chung and Cheng Wan-chien.

Yin Ju-keng's Career
Mr. Yin Ju-keng, nominal head of the group attempting to establish an autonomous regime in Eastern Hopei, has been Special Administrative Inspector of the Luanchow-Shanhaikuan Area of the Demilitarized Zone since 1933. In this position, held by Chinese mandate and Japanese tolerance, he has been the administrator for all practical purposes of the entire zone, since their is no corresponding official in the rest of the delimited area.
The son of a diplomat who served in Japan, Yin Ju-keng spent most of his early years in that country and acquired there both his education and his present wife. Returning to that part of China where his relations with prominent Japanese would be most remunerative, he obtained an advisory post in Marshal Chang Tso-lin's Manchurian army. He first became prominent when he associated himself with General Kuo Sung-lin's revolt against Marshal Chang. When that revolt collapsed, Yin took refuge in a Japanese consulate and later escaped.
Later he became a member of the entourage of General Huang Fu, acting in an advisory capacity as regards Japanese affairs. He was associated with General Huang when the latter was Mayor of Greater Shanghai in 1927-28 and accompanied General Huang to Peiping to arrange a truce with the Japanese in 1933. That truce resulted in the creation of the Demilitarized Zone and led to Yin's appointment as Administrative Inspector of one of the two areas comprising the Zone.—United Press.

Aid Asked Against Reds
Tientsin, Nov. 25.
Japan's collaboration in the war on Chinese Soviets was asked to-day in a telegram circularized by the newly formed East Hopei Autonomy Council for the Defence against Communism.
The appeal was sent to the Japanese Premier, Admiral Keisuke Okada; Gen. Yoshikui Kawashima, War Minister; Admiral Mineo Osumi, Navy Minister; Mr. Koki Hirota, Foreign Minister; Gen. Jiro Minami, Commander-in-Chief of the Kwantung Army; and Gen. Hayao Tada, Commander of the Japanese Forces in North China.
China will be completely sovietized by the Red forces, which have lately invaded Kansu, Shensi, and Inner Mongolia, if Japan remains indifferent to the situation, the telegram asserted.
"We request Japan to co-operate with us, by the immediate dispatch of troops to purge the area of Communists," the telegram concluded.

According to information received
here from reliable sources, a number of military trucks
carrying men of the former North East Army have arrived

Japanese negotiations.

Tung Nan Wan Pao published the following article on July 23 :-

IN A WAITING ROOM AT THE NORTH RAILWAY STATION.

A big, tall fellow stepped into the first and second class trains waiting room. He wore a suit of silk foreign clothing. When he walked into the room, a railway policeman gave him a salute. From his manner, he seemed to be either a senior officer of the railway station or a plain-clothes detective of the Bureau of Public Safety.
He entered into conversation with a man sitting on a bench, saying: "Ah, are you going to Soochow to inspect trains?"
"Yes," the other man replied, "I am waiting for the 9.30 a.m. train. Lan ..., you had a hard job yesterday."
"Ah," the big fellow went on saying, "what is national salvation really? It is only a blind disturbance! A crowd of people force their way into a station and demand for trains to take them to Nanking to submit appeals. We are all Chinese and we all love our country. But there are many ways of loving one's country and one should not resort to disturbances! Students should not abandon their studies or workers their labours because they want to make appeals to the Government. The Government is able to find some measures."
"You are right," the other man replied, laughing. They both laughed.
Their conversation made me recall what happened the other day.
It was about 94 degrees in the shade. Orderly columns of students, workers, girls and citizens marched in a grave but excited manner to the station singing and shouting the following slogans : "Rise! Let those who do not want to be treated like animals use their blood to wash away the enemy's tents! We do not fear death, we shall rush to the front! It is our glory to fight for our existence! Unite and advance, advance!"
They marched under the burning sun with sweat pouring down from their foreheads to their feet. Their blood was boiling.
When the marching columns reached the North Railway Station, they found the place already full of armed policemen. The columns remained for a long time under the sun without food and drink but they failed to secure a train.
"Reserve our energy to make preparations for a blood struggle!"
"Oppose the increase of XX garrison in North China!"
"Request our Government to declare war against XX!!"
"Recover the North-East lost territory!"
"Down with XX Imperialism!"
"Long live the Chinese Republic!"
After loudly shouting the above slogans, the mass left the station in great indignation. Numbers of motor trucks and ambulances containing policemen and detectives of the Imperialists and running-dogs stood by on Boundary Road.

The "Shengxozhsh"(生活知識) published the following article
in Volume 1, Issue No. 10 :-

RE ALLEGED USE OF VIOLENCE AGAINST UNARMED STUDENT
DEMONSTRATORS BY THE S.M.P.

On February 6, local newspapers published
a Reuter telegram from London reporting that in the House
of Lords on February 5 Lord Marley sought information
concerning the alleged use of violence against unarmed
student demonstrators by the Police of the International
Settlement of Shanghai in December last.
The so-called "unarmed student demonstrators"
probably refer to the Chinese students, but does it not
sound strange that no protest has been lodged by the
Chinese Government over the assault on the Chinese students?
In reality, there is nothing strange about it, because in
other parts of China where the "British Police" do not
function unarmed Chinese student demonstrators are similarly
treated with violence. Therefore, on what grounds can
China lodge a protest with the British Government?
The reply given in the House of Lords to
the enquiry put by Lord Marley undoubtedly means that the
Shanghai Municipal Police could not be blamed for using
undue violence because the conduct of the students had
gone beyond limits and bordered on disorder. The Earl
of Stanhope, Under Secretary of the Foreign Office, said
that the last thing that the Shanghai Municipal Council
would desire the Police to do would be to attack Chinese
unduly and raise bad feeling between Chinese and foreigners.
It is a pity that the argument of the Earl
of Stanhope, though smartly worded, is so silly, because
attacks on Chinese by the Police are public and common
occurrences. I have heard people say that at the time
when a Chinese student was arrested during a demonstration
in Shanghai, one of the Chinese policemen who was escorting
him raised his thumb and praised him thus:- "You are truly
courageous. Formerly 'sergeants'(?) used to attack
Chinese; one never hears of Chinese attacking 'sergeants'
......" Besides the attacking of Chinese, have not
reports appeared in newspapers of the throwing of a living
Chinese into a creek by two foreign policemen?

THE CHINESE REPUBLIC NATIONAL SALVATION FUND SAVINGS SOCIETY.

An organization known as the "Chinese Republic National Salvation Fund Savings Society"(中華民國救國金儲蓄會) has been formed by Kiang Vung Yue(江向漁), Yang Wei Nyoh(楊衛玉), Pan Niang Yao(潘仰堯) and Ho Ching Zu(何清儒) of the Chinese Vocational Educational Society(中華職業教育社).

The following are the rules of this Society:-
(1) Basic organization: Members of any public body, rural district, street, village, or family, not fewer than ten in number, may form a small body to be known as "---- Branch of the Chinese Republic National Salvation Fund Savings Society in ----- Hsien, ----- Province".
(2) District consolidated body: The various branches in a Hsien may be formed into a single body to be known as "----- Hsien or District Branch of the Chinese Republic National Salvation Fund Savings Society".
(3) A joint body formed by various branches of a Hsien or District is to be called "---- Provincial or Municipal Branch of the Chinese Republic National Salvation Fund Savings Society".
(4) A national body of such branches is to be called the Main Office of the Chinese Republic National Salvation Fund Savings Society.
Apart from collecting monthly and ordinary savings, this Society will also convene various kinds of informal meetings and consider reports submitted by executive members to promote common sense, to foster a national spirit and to encourage patriotic feelings. THE SHANGHAI INTELLECTUALS NATIONAL SALVATION ASSOCIATION
CRITICIZES MANIFESTO OF THE CENTRAL PROPAGANDA COMMITTEE
OF KUOMINTANG HEADQUARTERS

(Abridged Translation)

We are disappointed over the manifesto
issued by the Central Propaganda Committee of the
Kuomintang Headquarters on February 21. For the sake
of the Kuomintang and the future of the Chinese nation,
we beg sincerely to submit the following points for
consideration by the Committee and the authorities:-
The patriotic movement for the
salvation of the nation was started in Shanghai because
of the establishment of the bogus autonomous movement
in North China. At that time the traitors in North
China assembled numbers of opium addicts and made them
appear as representatives of the people in that territory.
The papers in North China openly published articles in
favour of the traitors. Yet the Central Propaganda
Committee failed to take any measures to rectify this
at a time when the activities of the traitors were
becoming highly dangerous.
Realizing our imminent danger, we
started the movement for national salvation and our
action was immediately followed by students throughout
the country. As a result, the traitors were alarmed and
their activities have since become less conspicuous.
If the Government officials and the members of the
Kuomintang are really sincere for the welfare of the
Chinese nation, they should support this movement.
Even if there exist irregularities in the organization
of the movement, they should take every step to rectify
them and direct the students in their movement.
Unfortunately, the Central Propaganda
Committee remained inactive while the traitors in
North China were actively engaged; but when the students
started a national salvation movement, the Central
Propaganda Committee adopted strong measures and
denounced the movement. This is why we are disappointed
over the manifesto of the Central Propaganda Committee.
We will all support our Government
if it will sincerely adopt a policy of resistance and will
frankly announce to the people its future policy. We
hope that our Government will not fall into its former
mistakes. This does not mean that we are demanding of our
Government to put up resistance against the enemy
immediately. What we earnestly desire is that the Government
will make all preparations for an effective resistance
against the enemy. In the past, not only had our Government
failed to arouse the feelings of the people or to organize
them to resist the enemy, but had, on the contrary, compelled
them to befriend the enemy. This is a suicidal policy.
If the Government fails to correct a
policy which will result in the ruin of China and the
annihilation of the Chinese race, then we can definitely
state that even if the Government has made all preparations
to resist the enemy, such preparations will result in
nothing.
In conclusion, we hope that the Central
Propaganda Committee will, in the interests of the Chinese
nation and the Kuomintang, immediately rectify its mistakes.

EMERGENCY MEASURES FOR THE MAINTENANCE OF PEACE AND ORDER

On February 20, the National Government promulgated the following emergency measures for the maintenance of peace and order:-
(1) When an incident that disturbs the peace and order or incites an uprising or obstructs traffic or endangers the nation in some other way has taken place, the military and police who are responsible for the maintenance of public safety may stop it by force of arms or by any other effective means.
(2) Whoever conducts propaganda by writing, drawing, speech or any other means may be arrested on the spot. In case of absolute necessity, armed force or any other effective means may be employed to overcome resistance.
(3) The military and police shall at once disperse any meeting or procession that is liable to impair the peace and order or to incite the people, and may arrest the ringleaders and other persons when they offer resistance.
(4) Whenever an incident of any one of the abovementioned nature occurs, the military and police shall at once disarm persons who are in possession of arms and arrest them. A search for suspects may be made.
(5) Whoever knowing a person to have violated these measures conceals him or accommodates him or makes him go into hiding may be arrested.
(6) When dealing with an incident, the military and police shall immediately report the matter to their senior officers. Arrested offenders shall be at once escorted to the senior officer of the Gendarmerie or the Commissioner of the Public Safety Bureau or the Magistrate of a Hsien or a Procurator for interrogation and the case shall be dealt with in accordance with the Emergency Measures for the punishment of persons endangering the Republic of China or under the Criminal Code.
(7) The military and police who deal with an incident in accordance with these measures shall accord special protection to law-abiding persons and pay attention to the maintenance of peace and order or to its restoration.

The "Holmes"(福尔摩斯) published the following comment on
February 8 :-

"UNWARRANTED USE OF VIOLENCE BY SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE".

In the House of Lords on February 5, Lord
Marley, leader of the Opposition, sought information on the
alleged use of force against unarmed student demonstrators
by the Police in the International Settlement of Shanghai
in December last. Replying, the Earl of Stanhope, Under
Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, said that the reports
he had read in the Shanghai newspapers concerning the
demonstrations there differed very materially from Lord
Marley's account of the happenings. It was obvious from
these reports that the students had disorganized traffic
and had tried to enter the Settlement. He stated that he
would inquire whether or not the Police under the control
of the Shanghai Municipal Council had used undue violence,
but he thought that the very last thing the S.M.C. would
desire the Police to do would be to attack Chinese unduly
and raise bad feeling between Chinese and foreigners. In
consequence, Lord Marley's inquiry was dropped.
This debate in the British House of Lords
is very interesting; it gives us two views of present-day
conditions in China.
In the first place, if a Chinese had been present
in the House of Lords during this debate, he would have
laughed heartily at the sight of the large number of British
Peers wasting their time and energy over happenings in China
to which an average Chinese citizen would not have paid any
attention whatever. Probably, Lord Marley had some ground
for his enquiry as to whether or not the S.M.P. had used
undue violence against unarmed student demonstrators in
December last. The reply given by the Under Secretary
did not definitely deny it, yet his assertion that according
to the reports of the affair carried by Shanghai newspapers
the students had disorganized traffic and had tried to enter
the Settlement is true. Thus the patriotic demonstrations
which took place on Nanking Road in December last had given
rise to two kinds of views: one to the effect that the
demonstrations were orderly, and the other that the students
had disorganized traffic and had tried to enter the
Settlement.
However, the opinion was general in the
House of Lords that "the last thing the S.M.C. would desire
the Police to do would be to attack unduly." We are also
certain that "the first thing the S.M.C. would desire the
Police to do would be to make justified attacks upon
Chinese" for that would not create ill feeling between
Chinese and foreigners but would produce "the utmost good
sentiment" among the upper class Chinese.
In the second place, if the patriotic
demonstrations held by unarmed students in China during
the past few years had been held in favour of the "friendly
Powers", the foreign and Chinese authorities would not have
dared to suppress them, but would have afforded every
protection to them. As the demonstrations were held
because of love for the fatherland, they were, in the eyes

4
February 10, 1936. Morning Translation.

of foreigners, "harmful to peace and order and constituted an attempted entry into the Settlement" and police batons should be used upon the demonstrators, while in the eyes of the Chinese authorities they were regarded as "riots" and "harmful to international relations" and had to be suppressed with swords, machine guns, stones, spies and imprisonment for the participants; furthermore, on the following day newspapers would publish reports to the effect that "the disorderly conduct of the demonstrators had bordered on the reactionary", that "thanks to efficient handling by the authorities, no untoward incidents occurred and the demonstrators had been quietly dispersed." The world on reading such reports will admire the efficient handling of the situation by the Chinese authorities. The newspapers which the Earl of Stanhope had read were probably Chinese newspapers and on this account he could base on them his statement to the world that the British gentlemen in Shanghai would never resort to the use of violence.
Frankly speaking, the attack made by the S.M.P. on the student demonstrators in December last was, in the eyes of the lower class Chinese, very mild and lenient and was far milder and more lenient than the action taken by the Chinese authorities against demonstrators. Supposing the students had not entered the Settlement and had demonstrated in Chinese controlled territory, the result would have been .......?
Therefore, we should shout "Support Imperialism!"

Anti-Autonomy Movement - activities of students
At 4 p.m. February 8, about fifty students from the
Chincn, Fuh Tan and Chih Chih Universities and the Tseng
Feng College (Chinese territory) assembled in Heng Feng Road,
Chapei, with the object of delivering open air lectures
on the national salvation movement. They carried a cloth
banner inscribed "Shanghai University and Middle School

flags showing maps of China with the Northeastern Provinces
outlined in red in contrast to the remainder of the country.

February 10, 1936.

Anti-Japanese slogans were shouted and sentiments against
traitors were expressed. Subsequently the propagandists
and a number of sympathisers formed a procession and marched
along Yung Shing Road, Jukong Road, and Paoshan Road to the
North Railway Station. Lectures denouncing Japanese
imperialism were delivered and slogans of a similar strain
were shouted. They dispersed about 7 p.m.

At 3.30 p.m. February 9, 1936, about 100 students
from universities and middle schools in the Western and
Nantao Districts of Shanghai assembled at the St. Catherine's
Bridge. They delivered open air lectures bearing on the
national salvation movement and subsequently marched in
processional order along Fong Zia Road, Chung Hwa Road,

police then began to disperse the students by force. The
crowd resented this and a free fight developed. Order
was eventually restored at 7.30 p.m. During the melee,
four policemen and the chauffeur of the police van were
injured, the latter seriously. A number of the rioters
also received minor injuries and seven were taken into
custody.

Min Pao and other local newspapers (Nanking Telegram) :-

DISCIPLINE IN SCHOOLS

On January 29 the Ministry of Education issued the
following instructions to the various Education Bureaux,
schools and colleges throughout the country:-
"Of late, students at various places have
demonstrated their patriotism and their anxiety for the
salvation of the nation. However, it is a pity that the
activities of a section of the students have been contrary
to law and unreasonable. This constitutes a violation of
discipline in schools, and as a result disorder
prevailed among schools throughout the country.
"Realizing their responsibility, the principals
of the various schools who came to Nanking recently have
issued a joint manifesto declaring that apart from
supporting the Government in preserving national territory
and devoting their attention to the promotion of education,
they are unanimously opposed to the suspension of studies
and the launching of movements that constitute a violation
of the law and the discipline of schools.
"In view of the importance of education and
the training of youths, General Chiang Kai Shek, President
of the Executive Yuan, on January 28 pointed out earnestly
and clearly the necessity of suppressing such undesirable
movements, the suspension of studies, etc. This Ministry
has been strictly ordered to observe these instructions
and to do its utmost to protect the educational work. It
should not be overlooked that education is as important
as the existence of the nation, and its suspension will
render fruitless the work of national salvation. It is,
therefore, evident that to remain away from school is
not an act of patriotism.

"This Ministry will carefully revise
the principles for national education in accordance with
the instructions of the Executive Yuan. The enforcement

work in accordance with the instructions of the Executive

Shun Pao publishing the following telegram from Nankirg:-
CHIANG KAI SHEK AND THE STUD NTS' MOVEMENT
ON Janua y 28, General Chiang Kai Shek,
President of the Executive Yuan, issued the following order
to principals of various schools through the medium of the
inistry of Education:-
"At this time of grave national crisis, the
educationalists should guide the youths in the observance of
disci line and endeavour to avert the crisis. In the recent
interview with representatives of school principals and
students, I stressed this point and also gave them an
explanation of the government's policy. The present
students' movement in various places arose out of the warm
patriotism of the students, but it was feared that sooner
or later they would go beyond the limits. At present certain
schools are completely without discipline and this eventually
resulted in a suspension of studies. Strict measures should
be adopted to rectify this situation.
"The winter vacation is now at end and all
schools will be resuming classes. The teaching staff should
persuade and guide the students in the right path and should
disqualify all students who fail to attend to their studies
or to pass the examinations. Students who attempt to
obstruct the studies should be instantly ordered to leave
the school, and no organization should be allowed to instigate
a suspension of studies or to interfere with the school
administration either within or without the school.. The
military and political organs in the district should suppress
all such organization. All this is intended for the
protection of education and to strengthen the national
force. The Ministry of Education should instruct all
Bureau f Education and schools to enforce this order
strictly."

Activities of local students in connection with autonomy movement
A number of students of local universities and
colleges who left Shanghai about one week ago for various
places along the Nanking Shanghai Railway Line for the
purpose of conducting propaganda against the autonomy
movement in North China, were compelled to return to
Shanghai by the Chinese authorities on January 28. They
were escorted from Soochow to Quinsan by a party of military
Police and from the latter place to Kiangwan by eighty members
of the paotui. The train in which they were travelling passed
through the Shanghai North Station in 2.30 p.m. and reached Kiangwan
about ten minutes later.
On leaving the train the students dispersed, but
shortly afterwards formed into processional order and, carrying
a cloth banner inscribed "Shanghai University and Middle School
Student National Salvation Propaganda Groups," marched along
Sui Dien Road, Chapei, to the North Railway Station. They
were joined by other students en route and at this time their
number had reached about one hundred. Leaving the North Station
at 5.20 p.m. the procession proceeded south along North Chekiang
Road until they reached North Chekiang Road Bridge where the presence
of a party of Municipal Police caused them to turn west along
North Soochow Road and back to Chapei via Kwang Foh Road. They
eventually dispersed on Kwang Foh Road to the west of stone
Bridge. During the course of the procession the students shouted
anti-Japanese slogans and distributed copies of two handbills
purporting to emanate from the Fuh Tan University Students
National Salvation Federation.
